description: Built-in language/tool starter entries used by the Library explorer (moved out of jcLibEmbedded.ts in 0.36.0).

entries.name: for
entries.description: Classic indexed for loop.
entries.longDescription: Useful when you need explicit control over the iteration index, loop bounds, or increment step.

entries.name: while
entries.description: Classic while loop.
entries.longDescription: Use when the loop condition is checked before each iteration and the number of iterations is not known in advance.

entries.name: do while
entries.description: Loop that runs at least once.
entries.longDescription: Useful when one execution must always happen before the condition is tested.

entries.name: switch
entries.description: Branch on an integer-like value.
entries.longDescription: Prefer switch when multiple discrete cases are easier to read than many if/else branches.

entries.name: struct
entries.description: Declare a structure type.
entries.longDescription: Groups related fields inside one aggregate type.

entries.name: typedef
entries.description: Create a type alias.
entries.insertText: typedef unsigned int MyUInt;
entries.longDescription: Common in C APIs to simplify function pointer, callback, or platform-specific type declarations.

entries.name: static
entries.description: Static storage duration or internal linkage.
entries.insertText: static
entries.longDescription: In file scope, static hides the symbol inside the translation unit. In function scope, the variable keeps its value between calls.

entries.name: const
entries.description: Read-only qualifier.
entries.insertText: const
entries.longDescription: Protects data or pointers from unintended modification and documents intent.

entries.name: volatile
entries.description: Volatile qualifier.
entries.insertText: volatile
entries.longDescription: Useful for hardware registers, shared flags, or memory that can change outside the current control flow.

entries.name: extern
entries.description: Declaration of an external symbol.
entries.insertText: extern
entries.longDescription: Used in headers to reference variables or functions defined in another translation unit.

entries.name: union
entries.description: Declare a union type that overlays several representations in the same storage.
entries.longDescription: A union stores several members at the same address, with only one active interpretation at a time. In C, unions are common in protocol decoding, register overlays, tagged unions, and memory-constrained low-level code.

entries.name: malloc / free
entries.description: Dynamic allocation pattern in C.
entries.longDescription: Classic heap allocation in C. Always check the returned pointer and free the memory exactly once.

entries.name: fopen / fgets / fclose
entries.description: Read a text file line by line.
entries.longDescription: Basic pattern for text file reading in standard C.

entries.name: fwrite / fread binary file
entries.description: Write and read binary data with stdio.
entries.longDescription: Useful for compact binary serialization or device-oriented data dumps.

entries.name: Header guard
entries.description: Basic C header include guard.
entries.insertText:
#ifndef MY_HEADER_H
#define MY_HEADER_H


#endif /* MY_HEADER_H */
entries.longDescription: Prevents multiple inclusion of the same header in a translation unit.

entries.name: C source skeleton
entries.description: Basic .c implementation skeleton.
entries.longDescription: Minimal source file structure for a simple C implementation file.

entries.name: Function with error path
entries.description: Function skeleton with centralized cleanup.
entries.longDescription: Common pattern in C when multiple resources must be cleaned up in one place before returning.

entries.name: Function pointer callback
entries.description: Callback typedef and registration example in C.
entries.insertText:
typedef void (*MyCallback)(int code, void *userData);

void RegisterCallback(MyCallback callback, void *userData);
entries.longDescription: Useful in embedded software, DLL exports, or event-driven APIs.

entries.name: function pointer declaration
entries.description: Declare a plain C function pointer and assign a compatible function to it.
entries.longDescription: A function pointer stores the address of a compatible function. This is the core mechanism behind callbacks, dispatch tables, plugin hooks, interrupt vectors, and many C APIs.

entries.name: pointer to const vs const pointer
entries.description: Distinguish read-only pointees from fixed pointer variables.
entries.longDescription: In C declarations, const binds to what is immediately on its left when possible. pointer-to-const protects the pointed value, while const-pointer freezes the pointer variable itself. This distinction is fundamental when reading API signatures and callback parameters.

entries.name: double pointer out parameter
entries.description: Return allocated storage through a T ** out parameter.
entries.longDescription: A T ** out parameter is the standard C pattern when the callee must allocate or reseat a caller-owned pointer. It is also common for handle factories, DLL boundaries, and functions that grow a buffer dynamically.

entries.name: function pointer parameter + context
entries.description: Pass a callback and an opaque context through a regular C function.
entries.longDescription: This is the smallest reusable callback API shape in C: a plain function pointer plus a void * context. It scales from simple loops to drivers, protocol decoders, GUI hooks, and asynchronous notification APIs.

entries.name: function returning function pointer with typedef
entries.description: Use typedef to keep function-pointer return types readable.
entries.longDescription: Raw declarations for functions returning function pointers become hard to read quickly. A typedef keeps state-machine handlers, ISR tables, and dispatch factories maintainable.

entries.name: array of function pointers
entries.description: Dispatch through a small table of C function pointers.
entries.longDescription: Arrays or structs of function pointers are the standard C technique for command tables, protocol handlers, and pseudo-object interfaces.

entries.name: void * user context cast in callback
entries.description: Recover typed state from an opaque callbackData or userData pointer.
entries.longDescription: Many C APIs, including GUI and instrumentation frameworks, pass a generic void * callbackData so the callback can recover caller-owned state. The normal pattern is to cast the opaque pointer back to the expected struct type at the start of the callback.

entries.name: CVI callbackData cast
entries.description: Read custom context passed through a LabWindows/CVI callback.
entries.longDescription: In CVI, callbackData is an opaque user pointer supplied when wiring the callback. Casting it back to a dedicated context struct is the clean way to avoid globals and still access per-panel or per-control state.

entries.name: InstallCtrlCallback with callback data
entries.description: Register a CVI control callback and pass a typed user context.
entries.longDescription: CVI callbacks become much easier to scale when the panel or control state lives in a context struct passed through callbackData. This avoids hidden globals and keeps multiple panels or devices independent.

entries.name: Win32 WNDPROC with user data in C
entries.description: Store a typed context pointer in GWLP_USERDATA and recover it in the window procedure.
entries.longDescription: Win32 often passes control through a C callback boundary. GWLP_USERDATA is the normal slot used to associate a typed application context with one window instance so the callback can recover object-like state.

entries.name: calloc / realloc
entries.description: Allocate zeroed memory and resize it safely.
entries.longDescription: calloc initializes memory to zero while realloc resizes an existing allocation. Keep realloc failure handling explicit when the original pointer must stay valid.

entries.name: qsort comparator
entries.description: Sort a C array with qsort.
entries.longDescription: qsort is the standard C sorting helper. The comparator returns a negative, zero, or positive value.

entries.name: bsearch lookup
entries.description: Binary search in a sorted C array.
entries.longDescription: bsearch is useful once the array is already sorted and repeated lookups matter.

entries.name: linked list traversal
entries.description: Traverse a simple singly linked list.
entries.longDescription: A classic low-level iteration pattern for intrusive structures and embedded code.

entries.name: popen / _popen
entries.description: Run a command and capture its output.
entries.longDescription: Handy for diagnostics tools, command wrappers, and quick system integration.

entries.name: POSIX pipe() read/write
entries.description: Create an anonymous pipe on POSIX systems.
entries.longDescription: Anonymous pipes are useful for parent-child process communication and short-lived IPC.

entries.name: Windows named pipe server
entries.description: Create a named pipe server on Windows.
entries.longDescription: Named pipes are a practical IPC option for Windows desktop tools, services, and test benches.

entries.name: pthread create / join
entries.description: Launch a worker thread with pthread.
entries.longDescription: The standard C threading API on POSIX systems. Add mutexes when shared state becomes more complex.

entries.name: Win32 CreateThread
entries.description: Create a native worker thread on Windows.
entries.longDescription: Useful when integrating with Win32 APIs that already rely on HANDLE-based primitives.

entries.name: pthread mutex + condition
entries.description: Wait for work with a POSIX condition variable.
entries.longDescription: Condition variables fit producer-consumer patterns and event-style synchronization.

entries.name: POSIX TCP client
entries.description: Connect to a TCP server on POSIX.
entries.longDescription: A compact client-side socket example for Linux and other POSIX systems.

entries.name: WinSock TCP client
entries.description: Connect to a TCP server with WinSock.
entries.longDescription: Remember to initialize WinSock before using sockets on Windows.

entries.name: sscanf parse
entries.description: Parse structured text in C.
entries.longDescription: sscanf works well for compact fixed-format records.

entries.name: key=value parsing
entries.description: Parse a key=value configuration line.
entries.longDescription: Useful for lightweight INI-style parsing without additional dependencies.

entries.name: clock_gettime
entries.description: Measure elapsed time with POSIX clocks.
entries.longDescription: Monotonic clocks are safer than wall-clock time when measuring durations.

entries.name: cross-platform sleep
entries.description: Sleep for a short duration in portable C.
entries.longDescription: Simple pacing helper for polling loops and console tools.

entries.name: _kbhit / _getch
entries.description: Read keyboard input immediately on Windows consoles.
entries.longDescription: Convenient for quick interactive console tools without a full event loop.

entries.name: system()
entries.description: Run a shell command and inspect its return code.
entries.longDescription: Small glue pattern for tooling, though dedicated process APIs are more robust for complex workflows.

entries.name: POSIX directory traversal
entries.description: Enumerate files in a directory on POSIX.
entries.longDescription: A lightweight directory scan pattern for Linux and UNIX-like systems.

entries.name: Win32 file enumeration
entries.description: Enumerate files with FindFirstFile on Windows.
entries.longDescription: Native Windows file enumeration helper for simple utilities.

entries.name: POSIX FIFO mkfifo
entries.description: Create a named FIFO on POSIX systems.
entries.longDescription: Named FIFOs are useful when two unrelated processes must exchange a byte stream without opening a socket.

entries.name: POSIX shared memory + mmap
entries.description: Create shared memory backed by shm_open.
entries.longDescription: Shared memory is useful for high-throughput IPC and real-time data exchange between local processes.

entries.name: POSIX semaphore
entries.description: Synchronize workers with a POSIX semaphore.
entries.longDescription: Semaphores are useful when a producer must wake a consumer without transferring ownership of a mutex.

entries.name: Win32 CRITICAL_SECTION
entries.description: Guard shared state with a Win32 critical section.
entries.longDescription: CRITICAL_SECTION is a lightweight intra-process lock commonly used in native Windows code.

entries.name: Win32 manual-reset event
entries.description: Signal work completion with a Win32 event.
entries.longDescription: Events are useful for one-shot notifications and thread coordination on Windows.

entries.name: select() readiness loop
entries.description: Wait for readability on a socket with select.
entries.longDescription: select remains a practical baseline for simple readiness-based I/O and socket timeouts.

entries.name: POSIX UDP socket
entries.description: Send a datagram to a remote UDP endpoint.
entries.longDescription: UDP is useful for telemetry, discovery, and low-latency fire-and-forget messages.

entries.name: POSIX termios serial open
entries.description: Open and configure a UART on Linux or POSIX.
entries.longDescription: A practical starting point for UART tools, embedded diagnostics, and serial-based test benches.

entries.name: Win32 COM port
entries.description: Open a Windows COM port with CreateFile.
entries.longDescription: This is the native Win32 baseline for serial diagnostics, board bring-up, and hardware test tools.

entries.name: simple log macro
entries.description: Prefix logs with file and line information.
entries.longDescription: A tiny logging helper can save time when building console utilities or early-stage diagnostics code.

entries.name: variadic function declaration (...)
entries.description: Declare a C function with a fixed prefix and a variadic tail.
entries.insertText: int LogMessage(const char *level, const char *fmt, ...);
entries.longDescription: In C, a variadic function must declare at least one fixed parameter before the ellipsis. The caller and callee then agree on a convention such as a format string, an explicit count, or a sentinel terminator.

entries.name: va_list + va_start + va_arg + va_end
entries.description: Consume a variadic argument list with the stdarg API.
entries.longDescription: This is the core C variadic-function pattern. The fixed parameter count tells the callee how many promoted arguments to read. The extracted type passed to va_arg must exactly match what the caller supplied after the default promotions.

entries.name: variadic wrapper forwarding to vfprintf
entries.description: Forward a ... argument list to a v* stdio function.
entries.longDescription: When a function accepts ... and then delegates to printf-family formatting, the correct target is the matching v* API such as vprintf, vfprintf, vsnprintf, or vscanf. You cannot forward ... directly without first materializing a va_list.

entries.name: sentinel-terminated variadic function
entries.description: Stop reading variadic arguments when a NULL sentinel is reached.
entries.longDescription: Some C APIs use a sentinel instead of an explicit count. This is flexible, but it is also fragile because the caller must remember to append the terminator with the correct type.

entries.name: va_copy reuse argument list
entries.description: Duplicate a va_list before traversing it more than once.
entries.longDescription: A va_list is a consumable cursor, not a rewindable container. If you need a second pass, copy it first with va_copy and then end both lists separately.

entries.name: struct shallow copy
entries.description: Copy a structure by value in C.
entries.longDescription: A plain assignment copies each field bit-for-bit. Scalar fields are duplicated, but pointer fields still point to the same underlying memory.

entries.name: struct deep copy with heap field
entries.description: Duplicate pointed data explicitly when a C struct owns heap memory.
entries.longDescription: This is a deep copy because the destination receives its own independently allocated character buffer instead of aliasing src->name.

entries.name: restrict-qualified pointer parameters
entries.description: Promise non-overlapping pointed ranges to enable better optimization.
entries.longDescription: restrict is a C contract saying that, for the lifetime of the restricted access, the pointed object is reached through that pointer expression family only. When the promise is true, the optimizer can vectorize and reorder more aggressively. When it is false, behavior is undefined.

entries.name: _Generic type-based dispatch
entries.description: Choose an implementation at compile time from the argument type.
entries.longDescription: _Generic is the C11 compile-time selection mechanism. It is the closest thing C has to overload resolution and is useful for typed macros, math wrappers, and API front-ends that keep a C call surface.

entries.name: X-macro + _Generic typed API front-end
entries.description: Generate a family of typed entry points and one generic dispatch macro.
entries.insertText:
#define SENSOR_NUMERIC_TABLE(X)     X(int, int)                     X(double, double)

#define DECLARE_PUSH(typeName, cType)     void Push_##typeName(cType value);
SENSOR_NUMERIC_TABLE(DECLARE_PUSH)

#define SENSOR_PUSH(value) _Generic((value),     int: Push_int,     double: Push_double )(value)
entries.longDescription: This pattern keeps one master type list and uses it twice: once to generate the declarations and once to build the _Generic dispatch. It scales better than hand-writing many similar wrappers.

entries.name: union for binary reinterpretation with memcpy alternative
entries.description: Overlay representations carefully and prefer memcpy for portable type punning.
entries.longDescription: Unions are often used for binary inspection, but aliasing and active-member rules are subtle across standards and compilers. When the goal is only to copy raw representation bytes, memcpy is the conservative portable technique.

entries.name: tagged union state machine payload
entries.description: Represent one of several payload shapes with an explicit discriminator.
entries.longDescription: A tagged union is the canonical C representation for a sum type. The discriminator tells the reader which union member is currently valid. This pattern is common in protocol parsers, UI events, and device state machines.

entries.name: bit fields for packed flags
entries.description: Store small integral fields inside one machine word.
entries.longDescription: Bit fields are compact, but their layout, signedness details, and packing can be implementation-defined. They are useful for local flags and documentation, but raw protocol or register layouts often still need explicit masks and shifts for predictable ABI control.

entries.name: flexible array member packet
entries.description: Attach variable-length trailing storage to a structure.
entries.longDescription: A flexible array member lets one allocation hold both the fixed header and the trailing variable-sized data. This is an important systems-programming and ABI pattern for binary messages, IPC blocks, and custom allocators.

entries.name: _Alignas / _Alignof
entries.description: Control and query alignment explicitly in C11.
entries.longDescription: Explicit alignment matters for SIMD, DMA buffers, lock-free structures, and ABI compatibility. _Alignas/_Alignof are the core language facilities in C11, while stdalign.h also provides the alignas/alignof convenience macros on supporting implementations.

entries.name: _Static_assert ABI contract
entries.description: Stop the build when a type layout no longer matches the binary contract.
entries.longDescription: Binary interfaces should fail fast when structure size or field offsets drift. _Static_assert is one of the most effective tools for locking down file formats, IPC packets, driver descriptors, and shared-library ABIs.

entries.name: strict aliasing safe type punning with memcpy
entries.description: Read raw bytes as another scalar type without violating aliasing assumptions.
entries.longDescription: Casting one unrelated pointer type to another and dereferencing it can violate strict aliasing rules. memcpy communicates a representation copy instead of an aliasing relationship, which keeps the code portable and optimization-friendly.

entries.name: container_of intrusive structure
entries.description: Recover the outer object from the address of an embedded node.
entries.longDescription: container_of is a classic intrusive-data-structure macro used heavily in kernels, runtimes, and embedded frameworks. It depends on a stable memory layout and should be paired with disciplined ownership and lifetime rules.

entries.name: callback with user context
entries.description: Pass both a function pointer and an opaque context pointer through a C API.
entries.longDescription: The callback-plus-context pattern is the workhorse of C APIs because it preserves state without globals and stays ABI-friendly across DLL boundaries. It is the standard answer when a callback needs object-like state.

entries.name: function table pseudo-vtable
entries.description: Bundle a set of operations into one struct of function pointers.
entries.longDescription: A function table is the C equivalent of a vtable. It is useful for hardware abstraction layers, test doubles, plugins, and protocol backends because behavior can be swapped without changing the public object layout.

entries.name: qsort-style comparator + context thunk
entries.description: Adapt a stateful comparison into a plain C callback API.
entries.longDescription: Many legacy C APIs accept a bare function pointer with no user data. A thunk or adapter layer is then needed to bridge toward a stateful comparator. On platforms that provide qsort_r or qsort_s, prefer the native context-aware variant when available.

entries.name: designated initializer for nested state
entries.description: Initialize only the meaningful fields of a complex aggregate.
entries.longDescription: Designated initializers improve readability in C by making field-to-value association explicit. They are especially valuable once structures get large, nested, or evolve over time.

entries.name: compound literal temporary object
entries.description: Create an unnamed object inline and pass its address immediately.
entries.longDescription: Compound literals are an underrated C feature. They provide a concise way to build one-shot objects for configuration calls, tests, or table entries without first declaring a separate local variable.

entries.name: volatile register block
entries.description: Model hardware registers as a volatile structure at a fixed address.
entries.longDescription: For memory-mapped peripherals, volatile prevents the compiler from eliding or merging accesses that correspond to real hardware transactions. This pattern should still be paired with explicit masks, barriers, and hardware-specific sequencing where required.

entries.name: register mask update with barrier
entries.description: Modify selected register bits without disturbing unrelated hardware fields.
entries.longDescription: A read-modify-write helper is common in embedded code because peripheral registers often pack several fields into one word. The barrier macro here is schematic, but the important idea is to preserve unrelated bits and respect the ordering rules required by the target bus and CPU.

entries.name: DMA-style circular descriptor buffer
entries.description: Manage producer and consumer positions in a fixed hardware-oriented ring.
entries.longDescription: DMA engines, UART drivers, and data acquisition firmware often rely on circular descriptor rings. The exact ownership rules vary by device, but the pattern is always the same: fixed storage, explicit producer/consumer indices, and clear full/empty conditions.

entries.name: big-endian frame encode/decode helpers
entries.description: Serialize integers explicitly instead of relying on host endianness or structure packing.
entries.longDescription: Binary protocols should define byte order explicitly. Reading and writing fields byte-by-byte is often safer than copying whole packed structs, especially across compilers, CPUs, and DLL boundaries.

entries.name: timeout with retry policy
entries.description: Retry a fragile operation until success or deadline expiry.
entries.longDescription: Real hardware and OS services are often not ready on the first attempt. A bounded retry loop with a monotonic deadline is usually safer than a fixed number of blind retries because it makes the time budget explicit.

entries.name: HAL / BSP / service split in C
entries.description: Separate raw board access, reusable driver logic, and application policy.
entries.longDescription: This pattern is common in embedded products. The BSP or low-level layer knows the concrete board, the HAL surface exposes only the operations the service needs, and the service layer contains the protocol or business rules.

entries.name: CAN frame descriptor
entries.description: Represent a classical CAN frame in portable C.
entries.longDescription: A compact CAN frame struct is useful for protocol stacks, diagnostic tools, and test benches. Keep the payload length explicit and avoid depending on compiler-specific packing when the frame is only an in-memory representation.

entries.name: SPI transaction descriptor
entries.description: Describe one SPI exchange with explicit TX, RX, and chip-select behavior.
entries.longDescription: Many embedded drivers model SPI exchanges as descriptors so the high-level code can describe a transaction without depending on one specific HAL call shape.

entries.name: CRC16 incremental update
entries.description: Update a CRC16 over a byte stream in C.
entries.longDescription: Incremental CRC helpers are common in UART, CAN, RS-485, and file-transfer protocols because the checksum can be computed as bytes arrive instead of requiring one contiguous buffer.

entries.name: versioned function table from GetProcAddress
entries.description: Bind one exported ABI descriptor instead of many unrelated DLL symbols.
entries.longDescription: A versioned exported function table is often more robust than importing many entry points individually. The host validates one ABI number up front and then uses the stable table for the rest of the session.

entries.name: ISR-safe byte ring buffer
entries.description: Exchange bytes between an interrupt handler and foreground code with fixed storage.
entries.longDescription: A fixed ring buffer is one of the simplest and most robust interrupt-to-foreground communication tools. In real firmware you must still reason about atomicity, IRQ masking, cache coherence, and single-producer/single-consumer assumptions.

entries.name: opaque handle API boundary
entries.description: Publish a stable C handle type while hiding the implementation details.
entries.longDescription: Forward-declaring the handle keeps the public C ABI small and stable while allowing the implementation to live in C or C++. This is one of the most common industrial interop techniques for DLLs, firmware services, and plugin boundaries.

entries.name: size/version negotiated config struct
entries.description: Make a binary configuration block extensible without breaking older callers.
entries.longDescription: Passing both sizeof(struct) and an explicit version number is a standard ABI-survival technique. It lets newer implementations detect what the caller understands and default missing trailing fields safely.

entries.name: multi-instrument bench context in C
entries.description: Aggregate instrument interfaces and shared state for a coordinated test sequence.
entries.longDescription: Test benches often orchestrate several devices at once. Grouping the instrument interfaces into one context object keeps dependencies explicit and makes simulation, replay, and logging much easier.

entries.name: __declspec(dllexport)
entries.description: Export a symbol from a Windows DLL.
entries.insertText: __declspec(dllexport)
entries.longDescription: Place this on a function or variable definition inside the DLL project.

entries.name: __declspec(dllimport)
entries.description: Import a symbol from a Windows DLL.
entries.insertText: __declspec(dllimport)
entries.longDescription: Place this in client code or headers used by applications linking against the DLL.

entries.name: __stdcall
entries.description: Windows stdcall calling convention.
entries.insertText: __stdcall
entries.longDescription: Often required by older Win32 APIs and some callback-based DLL interfaces.

entries.name: DLL export macro
entries.description: Windows export/import macro pattern.
entries.insertText:
#ifdef BUILDING_MY_DLL
#define MY_API __declspec(dllexport)
#else
#define MY_API __declspec(dllimport)
#endif
entries.longDescription: Typical pattern for one header shared by both the DLL project and its consumers.

entries.name: DllMain
entries.description: Minimal Windows DLL entry point.
entries.longDescription: Keep DllMain very small. Avoid complex initialization, loader-lock sensitive code, or thread synchronization here.

entries.name: Exported function
entries.description: Typical exported C function.
entries.insertText: MY_API int MyFunction(int value);
entries.longDescription: Simple export declaration suitable for a C-compatible DLL API.

entries.name: Exported callback typedef
entries.description: Callback typedef exported from a DLL.
entries.insertText: typedef int (__stdcall *MyCallback)(int code);
entries.longDescription: Useful when the host application must register a function pointer back into the DLL.

entries.name: Opaque handle API
entries.description: C DLL API based on opaque handles.
entries.longDescription: Good pattern to keep the ABI stable while hiding implementation details from client code.

entries.name: LoadLibrary / GetProcAddress
entries.description: Runtime loading of a C DLL on Windows.
entries.longDescription: Useful for plugin systems, optional features, or versioned binary interfaces.

entries.name: class
entries.description: Declare a C++ class.
entries.longDescription: Classes are the main building block of encapsulation and object-oriented design in C++.

entries.name: struct
entries.description: Declare a C++ struct.
entries.longDescription: Structs are like classes, but public by default. They are often used for plain data aggregates.

entries.name: enum class
entries.description: Strongly typed enumeration.
entries.longDescription: Prevents accidental implicit conversion to int and avoids enumerator name pollution.

entries.name: namespace
entries.description: Declare a namespace.
entries.longDescription: Namespaces group related declarations and prevent naming collisions.

entries.name: using alias
entries.description: Create a modern type alias.
entries.insertText: using StringMap = std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string>;
entries.longDescription: Often preferred over typedef for template-heavy code because it reads from left to right.

entries.name: constexpr
entries.description: Compile-time constant expression.
entries.insertText: constexpr int kValue = 42;
entries.longDescription: Marks expressions or functions that can be evaluated at compile time when possible.

entries.name: template<typename T>
entries.description: Basic template declaration.
entries.insertText: template<typename T>
entries.longDescription: Introduces a template parameter list for generic code.

entries.name: override
entries.description: Virtual override specifier.
entries.insertText: override
entries.longDescription: Requests compile-time checking that a derived class method truly overrides a base virtual function.

entries.name: final
entries.description: Prevent overriding or inheritance.
entries.insertText: final
entries.longDescription: Apply to a virtual method or a class to stop further overrides or derivation.

entries.name: noexcept
entries.description: No-throw function specifier.
entries.insertText: noexcept
entries.longDescription: Documents and enforces that a function is not expected to throw exceptions.

entries.name: extern "C"
entries.description: Expose C linkage from C++.
entries.insertText: extern "C"
entries.longDescription: Useful when a C++ project must expose a stable C ABI, especially for DLLs or plugins.

entries.name: nullptr
entries.description: Type-safe null pointer literal.
entries.insertText: nullptr
entries.longDescription: Prefer nullptr over NULL or 0 in modern C++.

entries.name: union
entries.description: Declare a union in C++ for tightly controlled overlapping storage.
entries.longDescription: C++ supports unions, but active-member and lifetime rules are stricter than in plain C when non-trivial members are involved. They remain useful for low-level storage, tagged unions, protocol work, and manual variant-like implementations.

entries.name: std::move
entries.description: Cast an object to an rvalue reference.
entries.insertText: std::move
entries.longDescription: Enables move semantics when transferring ownership or expensive resources.

entries.name: std::forward
entries.description: Perfect forwarding helper.
entries.insertText: std::forward<T>(value)
entries.longDescription: Preserves lvalue/rvalue category inside forwarding templates.

entries.name: Class skeleton
entries.description: Simple class skeleton.
entries.longDescription: Baseline class pattern with constructor, accessor, mutator, and private state.

entries.name: Abstract interface
entries.description: Pure virtual interface definition.
entries.longDescription: Useful for plugin systems, test doubles, hardware abstraction layers, and dependency injection.

entries.name: Single inheritance override
entries.description: Derived class overriding a virtual API.
entries.longDescription: Classic inheritance pattern with override for polymorphic behavior.

entries.name: Protected inheritance helper
entries.description: Protected helper members in a base class.
entries.longDescription: Shows how common implementation helpers can be exposed to derived classes while staying hidden from users.

entries.name: Composition over inheritance
entries.description: Inject a dependency as a member instead of inheriting.
entries.longDescription: Composition often keeps designs simpler and more testable than deep inheritance hierarchies.

entries.name: operator<< stream output
entries.description: Custom stream insertion operator for debugging or logging.
entries.longDescription: A common operator overload for human-readable logging and debugging.

entries.name: operator+ value type
entries.description: Binary arithmetic operator on a value type.
entries.longDescription: Useful for math types or other lightweight value objects where operator semantics remain intuitive.

entries.name: operator[] indexing
entries.description: Subscript operator for an indexed class.
entries.longDescription: Provide both const and non-const overloads so indexed access works in read-only and writable contexts.

entries.name: defaulted comparisons
entries.description: Use modern comparison defaults when suitable.
entries.longDescription: Modern C++ can synthesize equality and ordering when memberwise comparison is acceptable.

entries.name: Range-based for
entries.description: Iterate over a container with range-for.
entries.longDescription: The most readable pattern for simple sequential traversal of a container.

entries.name: Iterator loop
entries.description: Explicit iterator traversal.
entries.longDescription: Useful when you need iterator arithmetic, insertion positions, or compatibility with older code.

entries.name: Map traversal with structured bindings
entries.description: Walk through a map using structured bindings.
entries.longDescription: Structured bindings make associative container traversal concise and readable.

entries.name: std::find_if
entries.description: Search a container with a predicate.
entries.longDescription: Part of the standard algorithm library and often preferable to manual loops.

entries.name: erase-remove idiom
entries.description: Remove matching values from a sequence container.
entries.longDescription: Classic pattern for removing elements from std::vector and similar sequence containers.

entries.name: std::transform
entries.description: Transform one container into another.
entries.longDescription: Use standard algorithms to express intent clearly and avoid index-heavy loops.

entries.name: Function template
entries.description: Generic function template.
entries.longDescription: Simple example of generic code that works with multiple comparable types.

entries.name: Class template
entries.description: Generic class template.
entries.longDescription: Shows how a class can be parameterized by the stored value type.

entries.name: Concept / requires
entries.description: Constrain a template with a concept.
entries.longDescription: Modern C++ constraints produce clearer diagnostics and document template expectations.

entries.name: Forwarding function
entries.description: Perfect-forward to another callable.
entries.longDescription: Useful for wrappers, adaptors, or higher-order utilities that preserve value categories.

entries.name: Lambda capture by value/reference
entries.description: Basic lambda capture patterns.
entries.longDescription: Captures by value copy external state, while captures by reference let the lambda observe or modify external variables.

entries.name: Generic lambda
entries.description: Lambda with auto parameters.
entries.longDescription: Generic lambdas provide a concise way to write templated function objects.

entries.name: std::function callback
entries.description: Store a callback using std::function.
entries.longDescription: Good for callbacks with type erasure, though function pointers or templates may be cheaper in hot paths.

entries.name: free-function pointer alias
entries.description: Declare and use a plain C/C++ function pointer.
entries.longDescription: Ordinary function pointers remain useful for C interop, compact dispatch tables, and callback APIs that must avoid allocations or type-erasure overhead.

entries.name: pointer to const vs const pointer
entries.description: Read const placement correctly in C++ pointer declarations.
entries.longDescription: The same const-placement rules as C apply in C++. This is essential when reading library APIs, callbacks, and low-level code that mixes mutable and read-only views over data.

entries.name: double pointer out parameter for C interop
entries.description: Use T ** when a C API must allocate or reseat a pointer.
entries.longDescription: Even in modern C++, T ** remains important at ABI boundaries with C libraries, DLL exports, and hardware SDKs. Wrappers usually translate that low-level pattern into RAII types immediately after the call.

entries.name: callback parameter + void * context
entries.description: Define a reusable C-compatible callback signature in C++.
entries.longDescription: A raw function pointer plus a void * context remains the lowest-common-denominator callback shape for interop-friendly APIs. It is often preferable when you need a stable ABI and zero allocation overhead.

entries.name: function returning function pointer via alias
entries.description: Return one of several handlers through a named function-pointer type.
entries.longDescription: Named aliases keep advanced function-pointer signatures readable in dispatch code, protocol tables, and low-level framework glue.

entries.name: non-capturing lambda to function pointer
entries.description: Convert a non-capturing lambda to a plain function pointer.
entries.longDescription: A lambda with no captures can convert to a compatible function pointer. This is useful when modern local syntax is desired but the target API still expects a raw callback pointer.

entries.name: void * callbackData cast in C++ callback
entries.description: Recover typed state from an opaque user pointer passed by a C-style API.
entries.longDescription: Many C and GUI APIs pass a void * userData or callbackData so the callback can regain object or context state. In C++, static_cast back to the expected type is the normal, explicit pattern at the ABI boundary.

entries.name: CVI callbackData cast in C++
entries.description: Use callbackData to recover a typed context inside a CVI callback compiled as C++.
entries.longDescription: When a CVI project is built as C++, callbackData can still carry caller-owned context exactly as in C. Casting it once at the top of the callback keeps the handler clean and avoids hidden global dependencies.

entries.name: CVI callback dispatch to class instance
entries.description: Recover a C++ object from callbackData and forward the event to a member function.
entries.longDescription: This is the standard way to bridge a C-style CVI callback toward a C++ instance method. The static thunk satisfies the required callback signature, and callbackData carries the object pointer.

entries.name: Win32 WNDPROC to C++ object thunk
entries.description: Route Win32 messages from a static window procedure into a class instance.
entries.longDescription: Native Win32 creation begins in a static callback, but most real applications want per-window object state. The usual bridge stores this in GWLP_USERDATA during WM_NCCREATE and then forwards later messages to an instance method.

entries.name: Read text file with ifstream
entries.description: Read a text file line by line using std::ifstream.
entries.longDescription: Standard C++ pattern for reading UTF-8 compatible text files line by line.

entries.name: Write file with ofstream
entries.description: Write formatted text to a file.
entries.longDescription: Simple file output example using the standard stream API.

entries.name: Binary file read
entries.description: Read raw bytes from a binary file.
entries.longDescription: Convenient for loading firmware images, packed resources, or protocol captures into memory.

entries.name: stringstream parsing
entries.description: Parse tokens from an in-memory string.
entries.longDescription: Useful for simple text parsing when the data is already present in memory.

entries.name: popen / _popen command pipe
entries.description: Capture output from an external process.
entries.longDescription: Portable enough for many tooling scenarios when you need to capture stdout from another process.

entries.name: Windows named pipe client
entries.description: Connect to a Windows named pipe from C++.
entries.longDescription: Useful for local IPC on Windows between tools, GUIs, services, or test benches.

entries.name: POSIX pipe / read / write
entries.description: Basic anonymous pipe example on Linux or POSIX.
entries.longDescription: A small POSIX pipe example showing low-level IPC primitives.

entries.name: std::thread worker
entries.description: Launch and join a worker thread.
entries.longDescription: Basic pattern for running work concurrently. Always join or detach every std::thread.

entries.name: std::mutex with lock_guard
entries.description: Protect shared data with a mutex.
entries.longDescription: RAII locking with std::lock_guard keeps locking safe and exception-friendly.

entries.name: condition_variable producer/consumer
entries.description: Wait for work using a condition variable.
entries.longDescription: Use when one thread must sleep until another thread produces data or a stop flag changes.

entries.name: std::atomic flag
entries.description: Lock-free shared flag between threads.
entries.longDescription: Atomic flags are useful for simple stop requests or low-contention shared state.

entries.name: chrono duration literals
entries.description: Use readable chrono literals such as ms, s, and min.
entries.longDescription: C++14 chrono literals make durations explicit and type-safe. They avoid fragile raw integer delays whose unit is unclear.

entries.name: std::this_thread::sleep_for
entries.description: Pause the current thread for a relative duration.
entries.longDescription: sleep_for blocks the current thread for at least the requested relative duration. It is simple and portable, but it should not be used on a UI thread or in a latency-critical loop.

entries.name: std::this_thread::sleep_until
entries.description: Pause the current thread until an absolute deadline.
entries.longDescription: sleep_until waits until an absolute time point. It is preferable to repeated sleep_for calls in periodic loops because it limits accumulated drift.

entries.name: measure elapsed time with steady_clock
entries.description: Measure execution time with a monotonic clock.
entries.longDescription: Use steady_clock for benchmarking, timeouts, and elapsed-time measurements. Unlike system_clock, a monotonic clock is not affected by wall-clock corrections.

entries.name: duration_cast conversion
entries.description: Convert a chrono duration to a specific unit.
entries.longDescription: duration_cast performs explicit chrono unit conversion. Calling count() returns the numeric representation in the selected unit.

entries.name: deadline timeout check
entries.description: Check whether a monotonic deadline has expired.
entries.longDescription: Represent a timeout as an absolute steady_clock deadline. This is more robust than incrementing counters or repeatedly subtracting approximate delays.

entries.name: periodic loop without accumulated drift
entries.description: Run a periodic loop using an absolute next deadline.
entries.longDescription: Advance the next deadline by one fixed period and sleep until that absolute time point. This avoids the cumulative drift caused by sleeping for a full period after each iteration.

entries.name: condition_variable wait_for timeout
entries.description: Wait for a condition with a relative timeout.
entries.longDescription: wait_for blocks efficiently until notified, until the predicate becomes true, or until the relative timeout expires. Prefer it to active polling when another thread can signal readiness.

entries.name: condition_variable wait_until deadline
entries.description: Wait for a condition until an absolute deadline.
entries.longDescription: wait_until is convenient when several wait operations must share one absolute timeout budget.

entries.name: one-shot delayed task
entries.description: Run an operation once after a delay in a managed worker thread.
entries.longDescription: std::jthread is a C++20 managed thread that joins automatically when destroyed. This pattern runs one delayed action without leaking or forgetting to join a std::thread.

entries.name: cancellable periodic timer with jthread
entries.description: Run a periodic callback until a C++20 stop request is received.
entries.longDescription: std::jthread and std::stop_token provide a clean C++20 cancellation model. The absolute next deadline prevents periodic drift.

entries.name: reusable Stopwatch class
entries.description: Encapsulate elapsed-time measurement in a small utility class.
entries.longDescription: A reusable monotonic stopwatch is useful for instrumentation, profiling, communication timeouts, and test-bench diagnostics.

entries.name: system_clock wall-clock timestamp
entries.description: Convert the current wall-clock time to time_t for timestamps.
entries.longDescription: Use system_clock for calendar timestamps and logs. Do not use it for elapsed-time measurements because wall-clock time may jump after synchronization or manual adjustment.

entries.name: std::this_thread::yield
entries.description: Hint that the current thread can let another runnable thread execute.
entries.insertText:
#include <thread>

std::this_thread::yield();
entries.longDescription: yield is only a scheduler hint. It is not a delay and should not replace sleep_for, condition variables, or proper synchronization.

entries.name: standard timer design reference
entries.description: Choose the appropriate timing primitive for the required behavior.
entries.insertText:
/* C++ timing quick reference
   Relative blocking delay       : std::this_thread::sleep_for(duration)
   Absolute blocking deadline    : std::this_thread::sleep_until(timePoint)
   Elapsed time / timeout clock  : std::chrono::steady_clock
   Calendar timestamp clock      : std::chrono::system_clock
   Signaled wait with timeout    : std::condition_variable::wait_for / wait_until
   Managed cancellable worker    : std::jthread + std::stop_token (C++20)

   The standard library does not provide a universal event-loop timer object.
   GUI frameworks such as Qt and operating systems expose their own event timers.
*/
entries.longDescription: This reference clarifies which standard primitive matches each timing need. For GUI applications, prefer the framework event loop timer, such as QTimer, rather than blocking the UI thread.

entries.name: new / delete
entries.description: Raw dynamic allocation in C++.
entries.longDescription: Use when needed, but prefer standard containers or smart pointers in modern C++.

entries.name: new[] / delete[]
entries.description: Allocate a raw dynamic array.
entries.longDescription: Prefer std::vector for resizable arrays, but this pattern is still useful to understand older codebases.

entries.name: std::unique_ptr
entries.description: Single-owner smart pointer.
entries.longDescription: Preferred ownership model when one object clearly owns the resource.

entries.name: std::shared_ptr
entries.description: Reference-counted shared ownership.
entries.longDescription: Useful when multiple components truly share lifetime, but avoid it when ownership can stay simple.

entries.name: Custom deleter
entries.description: unique_ptr with a custom cleanup function.
entries.longDescription: Great for wrapping C handles inside RAII-managed smart pointers.

entries.name: RAII wrapper
entries.description: Resource wrapper releasing automatically in the destructor.
entries.longDescription: RAII is one of the most important C++ idioms for safe resource management.

entries.name: Windows keyboard polling
entries.description: Poll a keyboard key on Windows.
entries.longDescription: Useful for quick desktop tools, debugging helpers, or polling-style applications on Windows.

entries.name: Windows mouse position
entries.description: Read the current mouse cursor position on Windows.
entries.longDescription: Convenient when building small desktop helpers or diagnostics that need cursor coordinates.

entries.name: Linux keyboard input with termios
entries.description: Read a key without waiting for Enter on Linux.
entries.longDescription: Typical terminal trick for immediate key capture in console programs on POSIX systems.

entries.name: Windows message loop skeleton
entries.description: Basic Win32 message loop for keyboard and mouse events.
entries.longDescription: The standard event loop pattern for native Win32 desktop applications.

entries.name: try / catch
entries.description: Basic exception handling.
entries.longDescription: Use for exception-aware code paths when you need to report or recover from runtime failures.

entries.name: throw std::runtime_error
entries.description: Throw a standard exception with a descriptive message.
entries.longDescription: In C++, throwing an exception uses the throw keyword. There is no Java-style throws clause on the function declaration.

entries.name: catch and rethrow
entries.description: Handle locally, then rethrow the current exception.
entries.longDescription: Use throw; inside a catch block when you want to preserve the original exception type and stack unwinding context.

entries.name: exception translation
entries.description: Catch a low-level exception and throw a domain-specific one.
entries.longDescription: A good pattern when a subsystem should expose domain-specific errors instead of raw lower-level exceptions.

entries.name: custom exception type
entries.description: Define a small domain-specific exception.
entries.longDescription: Custom exception types can help separate categories of failures in larger codebases.

entries.name: std::optional result
entries.description: Return an optional value instead of a sentinel.
entries.longDescription: A nice alternative to magic values such as -1 when a result may be absent.

entries.name: friend
entries.description: Grant another function or class access to private and protected members.
entries.longDescription: friend is useful for tightly related helper functions, factories, tests, and symmetric operators such as operator<<. It does not make the friend a member of the class.

entries.name: scope resolution ::
entries.description: Qualify a name with a namespace, class, or the global scope.
entries.longDescription: The scope-resolution operator selects where a symbol comes from. In inheritance code, Base::Method() is the rough equivalent of Java super.method().

entries.name: Base::Method() call
entries.description: Call the base-class implementation explicitly from an override.
entries.longDescription: When Java would use super.run(), C++ usually uses Base::Run(). This works because methods live in class scope, not because there is a dedicated super keyword.

entries.name: Base constructor initializer
entries.description: Invoke a base constructor from the derived constructor initializer list.
entries.longDescription: This is the constructor-side counterpart to Java super(id). In C++, base subobjects must be built in the initializer list, not inside the constructor body.

entries.name: overloadable operators reference
entries.description: Reference list of the operator tokens that can be overloaded in C++.
entries.insertText:
/* Overloadable operators in C++
   Arithmetic / bitwise / logic:
     +  -  *  /  %  ^  &  |  ~  !
   Assignment / comparison / shifts:
     =  <  >  +=  -=  *=  /=  %=  ^=  &=  |=  <<  >>  <<=  >>=
     ==  !=  <=  >=  <=>
   Logical / increment / misc:
     &&  ||  ++  --  ,  ->*  ->  ()  []
   Allocation / lifetime:
     new  new[]  delete  delete[]
   Special forms:
     operator type()      // conversion operators
     operator"" _tag      // user-defined literals

   Not overloadable:
     ::   .   .*   ?:   sizeof   typeid   alignof
*/
entries.longDescription: This reference is meant as a practical checklist. Even when an operator is overloadable, it should only be used when the semantics remain unsurprising to readers.

entries.name: operator bool() conversion
entries.description: Implicit or explicit conversion to bool.
entries.longDescription: Conversion operators have no declared return type in their signature. explicit operator bool() is a common modern pattern for validity checks.

entries.name: operator double **() conversion
entries.description: Conversion operator returning a pointer-to-pointer type.
entries.longDescription: Yes, a conversion operator such as operator double **() is legal. It is usually reserved for low-level interop, because it exposes raw internal representation and can make APIs harder to reason about.

entries.name: C++ struct shallow copy
entries.description: Default copy behavior duplicates members, including pointer values.
entries.longDescription: The compiler-generated copy constructor and copy assignment perform memberwise copy. For owning raw pointers, this is shallow copy and often leads to aliasing or double-delete bugs.

entries.name: deep copy copy constructor + assignment
entries.description: Implement deep copy when a type owns heap memory.
entries.longDescription: This is a classic deep-copy implementation. In modern code, prefer std::vector<double> or std::unique_ptr<double[]> whenever you can, because they encode ownership more safely.

entries.name: rule of five owning buffer
entries.description: Combine deep copy and move support for a resource-owning type.
entries.longDescription: A type that manually owns raw memory often needs the rule of five: destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, and move assignment. Copy-and-swap keeps assignment concise.

entries.name: function template with auto return
entries.description: Generic helper that deduces its return type from the expression.
entries.longDescription: A compact template pattern when the exact return type depends on the operands. auto keeps arithmetic helpers and wrappers readable.

entries.name: class template with specialization
entries.description: Primary template plus one specialization for a specific type family.
entries.longDescription: Specialization lets a generic template adapt behavior or metadata for specific types without rewriting the whole interface.

entries.name: std::enable_if SFINAE
entries.description: Enable an overload only when a compile-time condition is true.
entries.longDescription: Classic SFINAE pattern predating concepts. It removes an overload from consideration when the condition is false instead of producing a hard error.

entries.name: if constexpr branch
entries.description: Select one compile-time branch inside a template.
entries.longDescription: if constexpr discards the non-selected branch during compilation, which makes generic code far simpler than old metaprogramming-heavy alternatives.

entries.name: perfect forwarding factory
entries.description: Forward constructor arguments without losing value category.
entries.longDescription: A standard pattern for wrappers and factories. std::forward preserves whether each argument was an lvalue or rvalue.

entries.name: std::span view
entries.description: Non-owning view over contiguous memory.
entries.longDescription: std::span does not own memory. It simply describes a pointer plus a length, which makes APIs safer and cleaner than raw pointer plus count pairs.

entries.name: std::string_view parameter
entries.description: Read-only non-owning text parameter.
entries.longDescription: std::string_view avoids unnecessary allocations when a function only needs to inspect text. The caller must still ensure the referenced characters stay alive.

entries.name: std::optional value flow
entries.description: Model a value that may be absent and consume it explicitly.
entries.longDescription: std::optional is good when absence is normal and not exceptional. It makes the empty case explicit instead of relying on magic sentinel values.

entries.name: std::variant + std::visit
entries.description: Type-safe tagged union with visitor dispatch.
entries.longDescription: std::variant is a safer alternative to manual unions and type codes. std::visit centralizes exhaustive handling of the active alternative.

entries.name: std::expected result
entries.description: Return either a value or an error object without exceptions.
entries.longDescription: std::expected, standardized in C++23, is useful when failures are expected and should travel with a structured error instead of an exception.

entries.name: std::any dynamic payload
entries.description: Store one value of any copyable type when the type is only known at runtime.
entries.longDescription: std::any is flexible but weakly typed compared with std::variant. Prefer variant when the set of alternatives is known in advance.

entries.name: std::unique_ptr ownership transfer
entries.description: Exclusive ownership that can be moved but not copied.
entries.longDescription: std::unique_ptr is the default smart pointer for single-owner heap objects. Move it when ownership must change hands.

entries.name: std::unique_ptr custom deleter
entries.description: Manage a non-standard resource with custom cleanup logic.
entries.longDescription: A custom deleter makes std::unique_ptr useful well beyond new/delete. It is a strong RAII tool for FILE*, HANDLE, sockets, and many C APIs.

entries.name: std::shared_ptr and std::weak_ptr
entries.description: Shared ownership with a weak observer to avoid ownership cycles.
entries.longDescription: std::shared_ptr is useful when multiple owners truly exist. std::weak_ptr breaks cycles and lets you observe an object without extending its lifetime.

entries.name: std::enable_shared_from_this
entries.description: Safely create a shared_ptr to an object already managed by shared_ptr.
entries.longDescription: Use enable_shared_from_this when an object must hand out shared ownership to itself. Constructing a new shared_ptr from this directly would create a second control block and is incorrect.

entries.name: std::vector reserve + emplace_back
entries.description: Preallocate capacity and construct elements in place.
entries.longDescription: reserve avoids repeated reallocations when you roughly know the final size. emplace_back constructs the new element directly in the container.

entries.name: erase-remove idiom
entries.description: Remove matching elements from a sequence container.
entries.insertText:
std::vector<int> values{1, 2, 3, 2, 4};
values.erase(std::remove(values.begin(), values.end(), 2), values.end());
entries.longDescription: For sequence containers such as std::vector, std::remove shifts kept elements forward and returns the new logical end. erase then shrinks the container.

entries.name: sort + unique deduplication
entries.description: Sort a vector and erase duplicates.
entries.longDescription: A standard STL pattern when order may be normalized and duplicates should be removed efficiently in place.

entries.name: unordered_map try_emplace
entries.description: Insert only if the key is absent and avoid redundant temporary construction.
entries.longDescription: try_emplace is often preferable to operator[] or insert when the mapped value is expensive to build and should only be constructed on actual insertion.

entries.name: find_if algorithm
entries.description: Search a range with a predicate.
entries.longDescription: Algorithms express intent clearly and work across many iterator-based containers. find_if is often cleaner than writing a manual loop.

entries.name: transform algorithm
entries.description: Map one range into another.
entries.longDescription: std::transform is the STL workhorse for element-wise conversion. It makes data-flow style code more explicit than a hand-written push loop.

entries.name: consteval
entries.description: Require a function to be evaluated at compile time.
entries.longDescription: consteval creates an immediate function. Every call must produce a compile-time result, which is useful for generated constants and validated metaprogramming helpers.

entries.name: constinit
entries.description: Require static or thread storage initialization without dynamic startup code.
entries.insertText:
constinit static int gCounter = 0;
thread_local constinit int tlsState = 0;
entries.longDescription: constinit is useful for globals and thread_local objects that must be initialized at compile time. It does not imply const; it only constrains initialization timing.

entries.name: variadic template + fold expression
entries.description: Aggregate any number of arguments with a fold expression.
entries.longDescription: Variadic templates model a parameter pack of arbitrary size. Fold expressions, introduced in C++17, let you reduce the pack compactly instead of writing recursive template machinery.

entries.name: C-style variadic function in C++
entries.description: Accept a classic ... argument list for interop-oriented code.
entries.longDescription: C++ still supports classic C-style variadic functions through <cstdarg>. They remain useful for ABI compatibility and printf-style wrappers, but variadic templates are usually safer and more expressive for C++-only APIs.

entries.name: recursive variadic template
entries.description: Consume a parameter pack recursively with a base case overload.
entries.longDescription: Before fold expressions, recursive variadic templates were the standard technique for processing a pack one argument at a time. They still matter when the algorithm is naturally recursive or needs per-argument control.

entries.name: perfect forwarding parameter pack
entries.description: Forward each argument with its original value category preserved.
entries.longDescription: Args&&... plus std::forward<Args>(args)... is the core perfect-forwarding pattern. It preserves whether each argument was an lvalue or an rvalue when forwarding into another constructor or call target.

entries.name: sizeof...(Args) pack arity
entries.description: Inspect the number of arguments captured in a template parameter pack.
entries.longDescription: sizeof...(Args) yields the pack length at compile time. It is frequently used in static_asserts, tuple helpers, overload steering, and template diagnostics.

entries.name: variadic generic lambda
entries.description: Capture a parameter pack in a lambda for lightweight forwarding utilities.
entries.longDescription: Generic lambdas can also be variadic. This is a concise way to build local adapters, tiny visitors, or debug helpers without declaring a named function template.

entries.name: concept definition
entries.description: Define a named constraint for templates.
entries.longDescription: A concept gives a semantic name to a compile-time requirement set. This usually produces clearer diagnostics and more readable template APIs than raw enable_if conditions.

entries.name: requires clause function
entries.description: Constrain a template directly on the declaration.
entries.longDescription: requires lets you state template constraints explicitly at the declaration site. In modern C++, this is often the clean replacement for older SFINAE-heavy signatures.

entries.name: CRTP static polymorphism
entries.description: Use the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern for compile-time polymorphism.
entries.longDescription: CRTP is a classic technique for static polymorphism. It avoids virtual dispatch when the derived type is known at compile time, but it also couples the hierarchy more tightly than runtime interfaces.

entries.name: std::ranges filter + transform
entries.description: Compose lazy range views instead of building intermediate containers.
entries.longDescription: Ranges let you express data pipelines declaratively. Views are lazy, so they usually avoid the temporary containers that classic algorithm chains often need.

entries.name: std::filesystem path + iteration
entries.description: Manipulate paths and enumerate files portably.
entries.longDescription: std::filesystem replaces a large amount of ad hoc platform-specific path code. It covers paths, metadata queries, directory traversal, and file operations with a standard API.

entries.name: std::source_location logging helper
entries.description: Capture caller file, line, and function without macros.
entries.longDescription: std::source_location is the modern standard alternative to passing __FILE__ and __LINE__ manually. It is especially useful in logging, assertions, and diagnostics helpers.

entries.name: std::jthread + stop_token
entries.description: Launch a joining thread with cooperative stop support.
entries.longDescription: std::jthread joins automatically in its destructor, unlike std::thread. Combined with std::stop_token, it gives a cleaner structured cancellation model for background loops.

entries.name: std::scoped_lock multiple mutexes
entries.description: Lock several mutexes safely with RAII and deadlock avoidance.
entries.longDescription: std::scoped_lock generalizes lock_guard and can lock multiple mutexes with a deadlock-avoidance strategy. It is the simplest modern choice when a scope must hold more than one mutex.

entries.name: std::atomic counter
entries.description: Use an atomic integer for lock-free increments.
entries.longDescription: Atomics are for small shared state that must be updated safely without a mutex. memory_order_relaxed is appropriate when you only need atomicity for the counter itself, not synchronization of surrounding data.

entries.name: compare_exchange retry loop
entries.description: Update shared state with a compare-exchange loop.
entries.longDescription: compare_exchange_weak is the foundation of many lock-free algorithms. On failure, current is updated with the latest observed value, so retry loops naturally converge on fresh state.

entries.name: lvalue / rvalue reference basics
entries.description: Contrast lvalue references with rvalue references.
entries.longDescription: An lvalue has identity and can usually appear on the left side of assignment. An rvalue is typically a temporary or expiring object. Distinguishing the two is central to move semantics, overload resolution, and efficient generic code.

entries.name: forwarding reference
entries.description: Use T&& in a deduced context to preserve value category.
entries.longDescription: When T is deduced, T&& is a forwarding reference, not just an rvalue reference. Combined with std::forward, it preserves whether the original caller passed an lvalue or an rvalue.

entries.name: reference collapsing rules
entries.description: Reference combinations collapse to a single reference type.
entries.insertText:
/* Reference collapsing rules
   T&  &  -> T&
   T&  && -> T&
   T&& &  -> T&
   T&& && -> T&&
*/
entries.longDescription: Reference collapsing is why forwarding references work. In practice, any combination involving an lvalue reference collapses to lvalue reference, and only rvalue-reference plus rvalue-reference stays rvalue-reference.

entries.name: placement new into raw storage
entries.description: Construct an object in already allocated storage.
entries.longDescription: Placement new does not allocate memory. It only constructs an object at a given address. You are responsible for providing correctly aligned storage and for destroying the object manually when appropriate.

entries.name: alignas / alignof
entries.description: Control and query object alignment explicitly.
entries.longDescription: Alignment matters for SIMD data, hardware interfaces, packed buffers, and ABI-sensitive code. alignas raises alignment, while alignof queries the required alignment of a type.

entries.name: standard layout / trivially copyable checks
entries.description: Validate whether a type is safe for low-level binary use.
entries.longDescription: These traits are useful when a type is mapped to a binary protocol, shared memory block, file header, or hardware register image. They do not guarantee a portable wire format by themselves, but they are a strong first sanity check.

entries.name: offsetof for binary structures
entries.description: Read field offsets inside a standard-layout type.
entries.longDescription: offsetof is useful in serialization, protocol parsers, hardware mappings, and low-level diagnostics. Use it only with standard-layout types.

entries.name: std::pmr::vector with monotonic_buffer_resource
entries.description: Back a container with a custom memory resource.
entries.longDescription: std::pmr lets you separate container logic from allocation strategy. monotonic_buffer_resource is useful when many allocations share the same lifetime, such as parsing, temporary graph construction, or request-scoped workspaces.

entries.name: custom allocator skeleton
entries.description: Minimal allocator type used by a standard container.
entries.longDescription: A custom allocator can route memory to a pool, a shared arena, a diagnostic layer, or a hardware-specific allocation API. In modern code, std::pmr is often simpler when you only need allocator configurability.

entries.name: static_cast / dynamic_cast / const_cast / reinterpret_cast
entries.description: Reference the main C++ cast families and their intended use.
entries.insertText:
/* Main C++ casts
   static_cast<T>(x)       // numeric conversions, upcasts, explicit constructor-like conversions
   dynamic_cast<T>(x)      // checked downcasts across polymorphic hierarchies
   const_cast<T>(x)        // add/remove const or volatile qualifiers
   reinterpret_cast<T>(x)  // low-level bit-pattern reinterpretation / address conversions
*/
entries.longDescription: Prefer the named C++ casts over C-style casts because each one communicates a specific intent. reinterpret_cast is the most dangerous and should remain rare in high-level business code.

entries.name: dynamic_cast checked downcast
entries.description: Safely downcast through a polymorphic base class.
entries.longDescription: dynamic_cast performs a runtime-checked conversion across a polymorphic hierarchy. For pointer casts it returns nullptr on failure. It is a safer alternative to unchecked downcasts when RTTI is available.

entries.name: reinterpret_cast peripheral register
entries.description: Map a fixed hardware address to a typed register block.
entries.longDescription: This is a typical embedded-systems use case for reinterpret_cast. It is powerful but ABI- and platform-sensitive, so it belongs in clearly isolated low-level layers.

entries.name: pointer to data member
entries.description: Store and use a pointer to a class data member.
entries.longDescription: A pointer-to-member is not a raw address. It identifies a member relative to an object of a given class type. It is useful in generic adapters, metadata tables, and reflective helper code.

entries.name: pointer to member function
entries.description: Invoke a class method through a pointer-to-member.
entries.longDescription: Pointers to member functions are distinct from ordinary function pointers because they require an object instance. They are useful in dispatch tables, state machines, and callback binding helpers.

entries.name: std::invoke on callable
entries.description: Invoke a function, lambda, functor, or member pointer through one uniform API.
entries.longDescription: std::invoke is the generic call dispatcher behind many modern facilities. It normalizes direct callables and pointers to members into one consistent invocation model.

entries.name: std::mem_fn member adapter
entries.description: Turn a pointer-to-member into a callable object.
entries.longDescription: std::mem_fn wraps a member function or member data pointer into a callable object. It is especially useful with algorithms and adapters that expect a normal callable.

entries.name: std::bind_front partial application
entries.description: Bind leading arguments and produce a smaller callable.
entries.longDescription: std::bind_front is the modern, narrower cousin of std::bind. It is usually clearer when you only want to fix the first arguments of a callable.

entries.name: std::tuple + structured bindings
entries.description: Group heterogeneous values and unpack them cleanly.
entries.longDescription: std::tuple stores heterogeneous values without defining a named struct. Structured bindings then unpack the result into readable local variables.

entries.name: std::apply tuple invocation
entries.description: Call a function with arguments stored inside a tuple.
entries.longDescription: std::apply is useful when generic code stores arguments in a tuple and later needs to forward them into a real function call.

entries.name: detection with if constexpr + type traits
entries.description: Select behavior from compile-time properties of the type.
entries.longDescription: A large part of practical C++ metaprogramming is not about exotic templates. It is about querying traits and steering code generation with if constexpr.

entries.name: static_assert interface contract
entries.description: Reject unsupported template instantiations with a precise diagnostic.
entries.longDescription: static_assert is one of the cleanest metaprogramming tools. It makes template requirements explicit and produces far better diagnostics than letting deeper errors leak out.

entries.name: std::bit_cast reinterpret bits safely
entries.description: Copy raw bits between trivially copyable types of equal size.
entries.longDescription: std::bit_cast is the type-safe, intent-revealing tool for bit reinterpretation between compatible trivially copyable types. It avoids many pitfalls of pointer punning.

entries.name: endianness with std::endian
entries.description: Branch on platform byte order when a protocol requires it.
entries.longDescription: Binary protocols, file formats, and hardware mappings sometimes depend on byte order. std::endian provides a standard vocabulary for that portability concern.

entries.name: std::byteswap for protocol values
entries.description: Reverse byte order explicitly when normalizing binary data.
entries.longDescription: std::byteswap is useful in serialization, communications, and low-level parsing code when you need an explicit byte-order conversion step.

entries.name: minimal coroutine task type
entries.description: Skeleton of a small coroutine return object.
entries.longDescription: C++20 coroutines are a language transformation, not a built-in scheduler. Real-world use usually builds on a framework, but understanding the promise_type skeleton is important.

entries.name: custom awaiter skeleton
entries.description: Define the await_ready / await_suspend / await_resume protocol.
entries.longDescription: A type becomes awaitable by exposing the coroutine awaiter protocol. This is the extension point used by asynchronous frameworks, timers, I/O layers, and schedulers.

entries.name: std::counting_semaphore
entries.description: Gate concurrent access with an explicit token count.
entries.longDescription: A semaphore models a pool of available permits rather than mutual exclusion over exactly one owner. It is useful for bounded resources such as ports, channels, or worker slots.

entries.name: std::latch one-shot rendezvous
entries.description: Wait until a fixed number of workers finish a phase.
entries.longDescription: std::latch is a one-shot synchronization primitive. It is ideal when a known number of tasks must all complete a preparation phase before execution continues.

entries.name: std::barrier repeated phases
entries.description: Synchronize several workers across multiple iterations.
entries.longDescription: Unlike a latch, a barrier is reusable. It is a good fit for iterative simulations, frame pipelines, and staged processing loops.

entries.name: RAII guard for HANDLE or resource
entries.description: Wrap a raw resource so cleanup is automatic and exception-safe.
entries.longDescription: RAII is the fundamental C++ resource-management pattern. Ownership is tied to object lifetime, so cleanup happens automatically even across early returns and exceptions.

entries.name: pImpl compilation firewall
entries.description: Hide implementation details behind an opaque pointer in the class definition.
entries.longDescription: The pImpl pattern reduces header dependencies, shortens rebuild times, and hides private implementation details from consumers while preserving a stable public interface.

entries.name: strategy via interface injection
entries.description: Swap behavior by composing an interface implementation.
entries.longDescription: Strategy is often cleaner than large conditional blocks when behavior must vary at runtime. In C++, unique_ptr ownership makes the composition explicit.

entries.name: observer with callback list
entries.description: Notify multiple listeners when a state change occurs.
entries.longDescription: Observer decouples publishers from subscribers. In C++, std::function plus a callback container provides a lightweight starting point for events and notifications.

entries.name: std::variant overloaded visitor
entries.description: Visit a variant with several lambda overloads.
