entries.longDescription: The overloaded-lambda helper is one of the most practical std::visit idioms. It keeps variant handling local, explicit, and type-safe without long visitor classes.

entries.name: std::monostate in std::variant
entries.description: Model an explicit empty state inside a variant.
entries.longDescription: std::monostate is useful when a variant needs a default-constructible neutral state, such as idle, unset, or not-yet-parsed.

entries.name: std::expected error propagation
entries.description: Propagate rich failures explicitly instead of throwing.
entries.longDescription: expected is most useful when failures are part of normal control flow. Returning std::unexpected keeps the error channel explicit and composable.

entries.name: std::source_location assert helper
entries.description: Report failing conditions with caller file and line automatically.
entries.longDescription: A small contract helper with source_location is often cleaner than scattering __FILE__ and __LINE__ macros. It is useful in diagnostics-heavy tools, test benches, and parsers.

entries.name: std::ranges iota + filter + take
entries.description: Build a lazy numeric pipeline with C++20 views.
entries.longDescription: This style is powerful for generators, index streams, and declarative iteration. The pipeline stays lazy, so values are computed only when iterated.

entries.name: std::ranges::subrange from iterators
entries.description: Wrap an iterator pair as a range object.
entries.longDescription: subrange is practical when legacy code gives you begin/end iterators but newer code wants a proper range to compose with algorithms or views.

entries.name: std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource
entries.description: Serve many small allocations efficiently from a pooling resource.
entries.longDescription: Pool resources can reduce allocation overhead and fragmentation when many small objects share the same lifetime. unsynchronized_pool_resource is intended for single-threaded or externally synchronized use.

entries.name: atomic wait / notify_one
entries.description: Block efficiently until an atomic value changes.
entries.longDescription: atomic wait/notify is a modern low-overhead alternative to condition variables for simple state transitions. It is especially attractive for flags, mailboxes, and compact synchronization points.

entries.name: std::atomic_ref on existing object
entries.description: Apply atomic operations to an already allocated scalar.
entries.longDescription: atomic_ref is useful when storage is imposed by an external layout, shared memory block, or mapped structure, but the access still needs atomic semantics.

entries.name: release / acquire publication flag
entries.description: Publish data with one thread and consume it safely from another.
entries.longDescription: The release store publishes prior writes, and the matching acquire load makes them visible to the consumer. This is one of the core synchronization patterns behind lock-free message handoff.

entries.name: extern "C" callback trampoline
entries.description: Bridge a C callback API to a C++ object instance.
entries.longDescription: Many C APIs expose a callback plus user-data pointer. The static trampoline pattern is the standard, ABI-safe bridge from that model to a C++ instance method.

entries.name: CAN frame + dispatcher
entries.description: Model a CAN frame and route by identifier in modern C++.
entries.longDescription: A small value-type CAN frame is a useful boundary object for protocol analyzers, test benches, and gateway code. Keep the wire encoding separate from the higher-level dispatch logic.

entries.name: framed protocol parser with CRC
entries.description: Assemble a binary frame incrementally and validate its CRC before dispatch.
entries.longDescription: Industrial serial and field-bus protocols should be parsed as explicit state machines. Length and CRC validation belong in the parser boundary so corrupted data never reaches the business logic as if it were trusted.

entries.name: Windows DLL ABI wrapper class
entries.description: Wrap a runtime-loaded DLL function table behind a small C++ RAII object.
entries.longDescription: A tiny RAII wrapper localizes LoadLibrary and FreeLibrary while the exported function table keeps the ABI flat and language-neutral. This is a good industrial compromise for plugins, drivers, and optional instrument adapters.

entries.name: std::unique_ptr for C API handle
entries.description: Own a C resource with RAII instead of manual destroy calls.
entries.longDescription: Wrapping a C handle in unique_ptr keeps ownership explicit and exception-safe. This is one of the cleanest C/C++ interop techniques for industrial APIs and legacy libraries.

entries.name: C-compatible packet with static_assert
entries.description: Validate a binary packet structure before using it across a C boundary.
entries.longDescription: For wire formats, shared memory, or C interfaces, verifying layout assumptions early is essential. The static_assert checks catch accidental ABI drift during maintenance.

entries.name: non-virtual interface (NVI)
entries.description: Keep the public algorithm stable while delegating one step to derived classes.
entries.longDescription: The non-virtual interface pattern keeps sequencing, invariants, and shared logic in one place while still allowing derived classes to customize only the intended variation point.

entries.name: type erasure wrapper
entries.description: Store unrelated callable-like objects behind one uniform interface.
entries.longDescription: Type erasure is the technique behind tools such as std::function. It is useful when runtime polymorphism is needed but inheritance should not leak into the user-facing API.

entries.name: function_ref-style callback view
entries.description: Pass a callable without owning it, to avoid std::function allocation and type erasure overhead.
entries.longDescription: A function_ref-style wrapper is a non-owning callable view. It is useful when the callee only needs to borrow a callable for the duration of the call, for example in hot paths, parsers, or measurement pipelines. The referenced callable must outlive the FunctionRef object.

entries.name: std::mdspan 2D matrix view
entries.description: View contiguous storage as a multidimensional object without copying it.
entries.longDescription: mdspan separates ownership from layout-aware access. It is a strong fit for DSP buffers, image rows, test matrices, and memory-mapped hardware regions when the underlying storage already exists elsewhere.

entries.name: generator coroutine with co_yield
entries.description: Produce a lazy stream of values with a minimal generator coroutine.
entries.longDescription: Generators are useful when you want lazy production of values without hand-writing an iterator state machine. They are attractive for token streams, scripted test sequences, and protocol decoders.

entries.name: single-producer single-consumer ring buffer
entries.description: Move data between one producer and one consumer without a mutex.
entries.longDescription: SPSC ring buffers are a practical lock-free tool for UART receive paths, acquisition threads, and streaming pipelines. They are much simpler and safer than general multi-producer/multi-consumer queues.

entries.name: ABA-aware tagged pointer CAS
entries.description: Associate a version tag with a pointer so CAS can detect pointer reuse.
entries.longDescription: The ABA problem appears when a pointer changes from A to B and back to A between two observations. A version tag lets the CAS distinguish a recycled pointer value from the original state. This is a classic technique for Treiber-style stacks and freelists.

entries.name: hazard pointer guard skeleton
entries.description: Publish the node you are currently reading before dereferencing it.
entries.longDescription: Hazard pointers are a safe memory-reclamation strategy for lock-free structures. A thread first publishes which node it may touch, and reclamation is delayed until no hazard slot references that node anymore. The algorithm has more machinery than shown here, but this is the core guard pattern.

entries.name: versioned C plugin descriptor
entries.description: Expose a stable plugin entry point with ABI versioning and function pointers.
entries.longDescription: For industrial plugins, a narrow C ABI plus an explicit version field is usually more robust than exporting C++ classes directly. The host can validate abiVersion before calling anything else and can reject incompatible plugins cleanly.

entries.name: host-side plugin version check
entries.description: Validate the plugin ABI before binding the function table.
entries.longDescription: Runtime-loaded plugins should fail fast on ABI mismatch. Checking the version before calling through the function table prevents hard-to-debug crashes caused by layout drift or stale binaries.

entries.name: driver interface with fake implementation
entries.description: Abstract hardware access so business logic can run against a simulator or test double.
entries.longDescription: This pattern is valuable for benches, drivers, and protocol stacks because it decouples device I/O from application logic. The same orchestration code can then target real hardware, a simulator, or a unit test fake.

entries.name: test step with verdict and log sink
entries.description: Represent a bench action as a reusable unit returning a structured verdict.
entries.longDescription: Returning a structured verdict is cleaner than scattering booleans and print statements. It improves traceability in automated benches and makes result aggregation much easier.

entries.name: framed serial protocol parser state machine
entries.description: Decode a byte stream incrementally instead of assuming full frames arrive at once.
entries.longDescription: UART, SPI, and TCP protocols often deliver data in arbitrary chunks. An explicit parser state machine is far safer than assuming each read contains one whole message.

entries.name: command object for bench action
entries.description: Encapsulate one equipment action so it can be queued, logged, and replayed.
entries.longDescription: The command pattern is useful when bench actions must be scheduled, undone, serialized, or replayed. It also creates a clean seam for logging and dry-run simulation.

entries.name: opaque C handle implemented by C++ class
entries.description: Back a stable C ABI handle with a private C++ implementation object.
entries.longDescription: This pattern keeps the external ABI in C while still allowing the implementation to use constructors, RAII, templates, and the rest of C++. It is a common compromise for SDKs, plugins, and instrument drivers.

entries.name: extern "C" factory with noexcept error boundary
entries.description: Prevent exceptions from escaping across a C ABI or DLL boundary.
entries.longDescription: Throwing across a C ABI is undefined territory in many real systems and is especially risky across shared-library boundaries compiled with different settings. Catch at the boundary and translate to explicit error codes.

entries.name: error code + output buffer boundary pattern
entries.description: Return status separately from produced data when exceptions and std::string are not ABI-safe.
entries.longDescription: C ABIs should avoid returning std::string, exceptions, or allocator-owned memory unless ownership rules are extremely explicit. A caller-provided buffer keeps the lifetime model obvious and language-neutral.

entries.name: size/version ABI negotiation
entries.description: Accept older or newer struct layouts by checking size and version first.
entries.longDescription: Version-tagged option structures are a standard long-term ABI maintenance technique. They let a DLL evolve without forcing every consumer to rebuild immediately.

entries.name: std::span<std::byte> over C buffer
entries.description: Wrap a raw C pointer and length with a safer non-owning view in C++ code.
entries.longDescription: span is a good C++ adaptation layer on top of C buffers because it adds size information without taking ownership. It is particularly useful in protocol parsers, DMA wrappers, and binary APIs.

entries.name: driver HAL / service layering in C++
entries.description: Separate hardware access, reusable protocol logic, and application orchestration.
entries.longDescription: Keeping the HAL narrow and the service logic independent from board code is one of the cleanest ways to obtain reusable protocol code, simulation hooks, and unit-test seams in C++ firmware and instrument control software.

entries.name: retry policy with bounded backoff
entries.description: Retry transient hardware or transport faults without creating an infinite loop.
entries.longDescription: Hardware discovery, serial links, and field instruments often fail transiently. A bounded retry policy with explicit backoff is usually safer than duplicating ad hoc retry loops across the codebase.

entries.name: bench orchestrator with typed instruments
entries.description: Coordinate several instruments through one high-level test sequence object.
entries.longDescription: A bench orchestrator expresses the test intent at a higher level than raw SCPI or driver calls. It makes sequencing, simulation, and reporting clearer in automated validation software.

entries.name: exported C plugin descriptor from C++
entries.description: Publish a versioned function table that a pure C host can consume safely.
entries.longDescription: A versioned exported function table is often simpler and more stable than exporting many unrelated symbols. Hosts can validate the descriptor once, then call through a narrow ABI that survives internal C++ refactoring.

entries.name: raw pointer T *
entries.description: Declare a raw pointer.
entries.longDescription: Use raw pointers mainly as non-owning observers, optional references, low-level handles or C interoperability boundaries.

entries.name: pointer to const: const T *
entries.description: Reseatable pointer that cannot modify its pointee.
entries.longDescription: Read from right to left: pointerToConst is a pointer to a const int.

entries.name: const pointer: T * const
entries.description: Fixed pointer that can modify its pointee.
entries.longDescription: Read from right to left: constPointer is a const pointer to an int.

entries.name: const pointer to const: const T * const
entries.description: Fixed pointer to a read-only pointee.
entries.longDescription: Both levels are const: the object is read-only through this pointer and the pointer variable cannot be reseated.

entries.name: pointer const reading rule
entries.description: Reference guide for reading const pointer declarations.
entries.insertText:
/*
 T *p;               pointer to T
 const T *p;         pointer to const T
 T const *p;         pointer to const T
 T * const p;        const pointer to T
 const T * const p;  const pointer to const T
 T **p;              pointer to pointer to T
*/
entries.longDescription: Read declarations from the variable name outward.

entries.name: pointer to pointer: T **
entries.description: Use double indirection, often for C out parameters.
entries.longDescription: When you control a modern C++ interface, prefer returning a container or smart pointer.

entries.name: reference and const reference
entries.description: Use references for mandatory aliases.
entries.insertText:
void Update(Device &device);
void Print(const Device &device);
entries.longDescription: A reference normally expresses a required non-null object. const T & avoids copying while blocking writes through the reference.

entries.name: rvalue reference T &&
entries.description: Consume movable temporary objects.
entries.longDescription: Rvalue references underpin move construction, move assignment and consuming overloads.

entries.name: non-owning observer raw pointer
entries.description: Document a nullable pointer that does not own lifetime.
entries.longDescription: Use a reference instead when null is forbidden.

entries.name: std::unique_ptr with std::make_unique
entries.description: Represent exclusive ownership.
entries.longDescription: std::unique_ptr is the preferred default owning pointer. It moves but does not copy.

entries.name: std::unique_ptr<T[]> array
entries.description: Own a fixed-size dynamic array.
entries.longDescription: Prefer std::vector for general resizable sequences.

entries.name: transfer std::unique_ptr ownership
entries.description: Move exclusive ownership.
entries.longDescription: After std::move, the source unique_ptr remains valid but is normally empty.

entries.name: std::shared_ptr with std::make_shared
entries.description: Represent genuine shared lifetime ownership.
entries.longDescription: Use shared_ptr only when several components truly own the same lifetime.

entries.name: std::weak_ptr lock
entries.description: Observe shared state without extending lifetime.
entries.longDescription: weak_ptr avoids ownership extension and can break cycles.

entries.name: break shared_ptr cycle with weak_ptr
entries.description: Use weak_ptr for a non-owning back-reference.
entries.longDescription: A pair of mutual shared_ptr references would prevent destruction because neither count reaches zero.

entries.name: const smart pointer vs smart pointer to const
entries.description: Distinguish wrapper constness from pointee constness.
entries.longDescription: std::unique_ptr<const T> owns a read-only T. const std::unique_ptr<T> freezes reset/move on that variable while T remains mutable.

entries.name: smart pointer selection reference
entries.description: Choose the ownership representation.
entries.insertText:
/*
 std::unique_ptr<T> : one owner; preferred owning pointer
 std::shared_ptr<T> : several genuine owners
 std::weak_ptr<T>   : observer of shared_ptr-managed object
 T *                : optional non-owning observer / interop
 T &                : mandatory non-owning alias
 std::vector<T>     : preferred resizable owned sequence
*/
entries.longDescription: Start with values, containers and unique_ptr. Introduce shared_ptr only when the ownership graph needs it.

entries.name: Java super() equivalent: base constructor initializer
entries.description: Initialize the base subobject from a derived constructor.
entries.longDescription: C++ has no super() keyword. Write Base(arguments) in the derived constructor initializer list.

entries.name: Java super.method() equivalent: Base::Method()
entries.description: Call a specific base implementation.
entries.longDescription: C++ uses scope resolution with the base-class name rather than super.method().

entries.name: Java instanceof equivalent: dynamic_cast pointer
entries.description: Check a runtime derived type through a polymorphic base pointer.
entries.longDescription: This is the closest direct equivalent of object instanceof Sensor. The base must be polymorphic, normally by declaring at least one virtual function.

entries.name: dynamic_cast reference throws std::bad_cast
entries.description: Checked downcast when a reference is required.
entries.longDescription: A failed pointer cast returns nullptr. A failed reference cast throws std::bad_cast.

entries.name: typeid exact runtime type check
entries.description: Compare the exact dynamic type.
entries.longDescription: typeid checks an exact type; dynamic_cast also matches derived classes.

entries.name: virtual dispatch instead of instanceof
entries.description: Prefer polymorphism when behavior varies by derived type.
entries.longDescription: Repeated instanceof-style branches often indicate that the operation belongs in a virtual member function.

entries.name: std::holds_alternative for std::variant
entries.description: Check an alternative in a closed type-safe union.
entries.longDescription: For a closed known type set, std::variant can be safer than RTTI.

entries.name: std::is_base_of_v compile-time relationship
entries.description: Check inheritance at compile time.
entries.insertText:
#include <type_traits>

static_assert(std::is_base_of_v<Device, Sensor>);
entries.longDescription: This differs from instanceof: it asks a compile-time question about types, not a runtime object.

entries.name: Java-to-C++ inheritance quick reference
entries.description: Reference map for common Java spellings.
entries.longDescription: C++ expresses the same concepts with explicit base names, virtual functions, RTTI and scope resolution.

entries.name: Container selection quick reference
entries.description: Choose a sequence container according to storage, iterator stability, and mutation needs.
entries.insertText:
/*
 std::array<T, N>       fixed-size contiguous storage
 std::vector<T>         resizable contiguous storage; default sequence choice
 std::deque<T>          fast insertion/removal at both ends
 std::list<T>           stable iterators; O(1) splice/erase with iterator
 std::forward_list<T>   compact singly-linked list
 std::string            owning text buffer
 std::string_view       non-owning read-only text view
 std::span<T>           non-owning contiguous range view (C++20)
*/
entries.longDescription: Use std::vector by default for general sequences. Reach for list-like containers only when their specific iterator-stability or splice properties matter.

entries.name: std::array fixed-size container
entries.description: Store a fixed number of elements with container semantics.
entries.longDescription: std::array owns inline fixed-size storage and supports begin/end, size, at, front, back, and data.

entries.name: std::array fill and data
entries.description: Fill fixed storage and expose a contiguous data pointer.
entries.longDescription: Useful for protocol buffers and hardware-facing APIs that expect pointer plus length.

entries.name: std::vector basics
entries.description: Use the default resizable contiguous sequence container.
entries.longDescription: std::vector is generally the first container to consider for dynamic sequences because it is cache-friendly and integrates well with STL algorithms.

entries.name: std::vector reserve capacity resize
entries.description: Distinguish vector size from allocated capacity.
entries.longDescription: reserve avoids repeated reallocations when the approximate final number of elements is known. resize changes the logical number of elements.

entries.name: std::vector access at data front back
entries.description: Use the main vector element-access methods.
entries.longDescription: at throws std::out_of_range on invalid index. operator[] does not perform bounds checking.

entries.name: std::vector insert erase range
entries.description: Insert or erase vector elements by iterator position or range.
entries.longDescription: Insertion and erasure can invalidate iterators and references because vector elements may move.

entries.name: std::erase_if vector C++20
entries.description: Remove matching vector elements with the C++20 helper.
entries.longDescription: std::erase_if is the concise C++20 replacement for the classic erase-remove idiom on standard sequence containers.

entries.name: std::deque push front and back
entries.description: Use a double-ended queue with efficient operations at both ends.
entries.longDescription: std::deque is useful for sliding windows, work queues, and buffers that need push/pop at both front and back.

entries.name: std::list insert erase splice
entries.description: Use linked-list splice and iterator-safe erasure.
entries.longDescription: std::list provides stable iterators for unaffected elements and constant-time node splicing, but it has weaker cache locality than vector.

entries.name: std::list sort unique remove_if
entries.description: Use list-specific algorithms that relink nodes.
entries.longDescription: std::list exposes member algorithms because generic algorithms such as std::sort require random-access iterators.

entries.name: std::forward_list insert_after erase_after
entries.description: Manipulate a singly-linked list through before-position iterators.
entries.longDescription: std::forward_list minimizes node overhead but only supports forward traversal and after-position insertion/erasure.

entries.name: std::string common methods
entries.description: Use common owning string operations.
entries.longDescription: starts_with and ends_with are available in C++20. std::string manages its own writable contiguous character storage.

entries.name: std::string_view non-owning view
entries.description: Pass read-only text without allocating or copying.
entries.longDescription: std::string_view does not own its characters. Ensure the referenced buffer outlives the view.

entries.name: std::span contiguous view C++20
entries.description: Expose a non-owning view over contiguous elements.
entries.longDescription: std::span works with arrays, vectors, and pointer-size pairs while preserving size information.

entries.name: std::bitset fixed bit flags
entries.description: Store a compile-time fixed number of bits.
entries.longDescription: std::bitset is not a general STL container, but it is useful for fixed flag fields, masks, and diagnostics.

entries.name: Ordered associative selection quick reference
entries.description: Choose ordered tree-based associative containers.
entries.insertText:
/*
 std::set<Key>              unique sorted keys
 std::multiset<Key>         sorted keys with duplicates
 std::map<Key, Value>       unique sorted key/value pairs
 std::multimap<Key, Value>  sorted key/value pairs with duplicate keys

 Typical lookup cost: logarithmic.
 Use when sorted iteration, lower_bound, or range queries matter.
*/
entries.longDescription: Ordered associative containers maintain key ordering and expose lower_bound, upper_bound, and equal_range.

entries.name: std::set insert contains find erase
entries.description: Manage unique sorted keys.
entries.longDescription: std::set stores each key once and keeps iteration ordered according to its comparator.

entries.name: std::multiset duplicates equal_range
entries.description: Store sorted duplicate keys and traverse one equivalent-key range.
entries.longDescription: std::multiset preserves all duplicates. count and equal_range are useful when grouping equal values.

entries.name: std::map insert access try_emplace
entries.description: Store unique sorted key/value pairs and use modern insertion helpers.
entries.longDescription: operator[] may default-construct a mapped value. try_emplace avoids constructing the mapped value when the key already exists.

entries.name: std::map find contains at erase
entries.description: Perform safe ordered-map lookup and erasure.
entries.longDescription: find does not insert. at provides checked access and throws when the key is missing.

entries.name: std::multimap duplicate keys
entries.description: Store multiple mapped values for one ordered key.
entries.longDescription: Use std::multimap when duplicate keys are meaningful and ordered grouping is desirable.

entries.name: lower_bound upper_bound equal_range
entries.description: Perform ordered boundary and range searches.
entries.longDescription: Boundary-search methods are a major reason to choose an ordered associative container over an unordered hash table.

entries.name: std::map custom comparator
entries.description: Provide an ordering policy for ordered containers.
entries.longDescription: A comparator defines key equivalence and ordering. It must satisfy strict weak ordering.

entries.name: Unordered associative selection quick reference
entries.description: Choose hash-table associative containers.
entries.insertText:
/*
 std::unordered_set<Key>              unique hashed keys
 std::unordered_multiset<Key>         hashed keys with duplicates
 std::unordered_map<Key, Value>       unique hashed key/value pairs
 std::unordered_multimap<Key, Value>  hashed key/value pairs with duplicate keys

 Average lookup cost is typically constant-time.
 Iteration order is unspecified and can change after rehash.
*/
entries.longDescription: Use unordered containers for key-based lookup when sorted iteration and ordered range queries are not required.

entries.name: std::unordered_set insert contains erase
entries.description: Manage unique hashed keys.
entries.longDescription: unordered_set provides efficient average-case key lookup without sorted traversal.

entries.name: std::unordered_multiset duplicates
entries.description: Store duplicate hashed keys.
entries.longDescription: unordered_multiset groups equivalent values into ranges but does not guarantee global iteration order.

entries.name: std::unordered_map basics
entries.description: Store unique hashed key/value pairs.
entries.longDescription: unordered_map is a common choice for fast dictionary-style lookup when key ordering is irrelevant.

entries.name: unordered_map find contains at erase
entries.description: Use non-inserting lookup and erasure on a hash map.
entries.longDescription: Prefer find, contains, or at when a missing key should not silently create a new mapped value.

entries.name: std::unordered_multimap duplicate keys
entries.description: Store several hashed values for one key.
entries.longDescription: Use equal_range to process all values associated with a duplicate key.

entries.name: reserve rehash load_factor
entries.description: Tune hash-table capacity and inspect its load.
entries.longDescription: reserve can reduce rehash operations when the approximate number of elements is known. Rehash invalidates iterators.

entries.name: custom hash for struct key
entries.description: Provide equality and hashing for a custom key type.
entries.longDescription: A hash function should be stable for the lifetime of a key stored in the table and should distribute values reasonably.

entries.name: unordered iteration and invalidation reminder
entries.description: Document the main unordered-container pitfalls.
entries.insertText:
/*
 unordered_* iteration order is unspecified.
 Rehashing invalidates iterators.
 References and pointers to stored elements remain valid across rehash,
 but erasing an element invalidates references and pointers to that element.
 Do not rely on output ordering for logs or serialized files.
*/
entries.longDescription: Use an ordered container or sort extracted keys when deterministic iteration order is required.

entries.name: Container adaptor selection quick reference
entries.description: Choose a restricted queue-like interface when full container traversal is unnecessary.
entries.insertText:
/*
 std::stack<T>          LIFO access: push, pop, top
 std::queue<T>          FIFO access: push, pop, front, back
 std::priority_queue<T> highest-priority access: push, pop, top

 Adaptors deliberately expose a restricted interface.
*/
entries.longDescription: Container adaptors express access policy clearly and prevent accidental arbitrary mutation.

entries.name: std::stack LIFO
entries.description: Use last-in-first-out storage.
entries.longDescription: std::stack is suitable for parsing, undo state, depth-first traversal, and explicit work stacks.

entries.name: std::queue FIFO
entries.description: Use first-in-first-out storage.
entries.longDescription: std::queue is suitable for event processing and breadth-first work scheduling.

entries.name: std::priority_queue max heap
entries.description: Use a max-priority queue.
entries.longDescription: std::priority_queue exposes the highest-priority element at top by default.

entries.name: std::priority_queue min heap comparator
entries.description: Invert the comparator to create a min-priority queue.
entries.longDescription: The underlying sequence defaults to std::vector. The comparator defines which element appears at top.

entries.name: Iterator category quick reference
entries.description: Understand iterator capability levels.
entries.insertText:
/*
 input iterator         read a single-pass sequence
 output iterator        write a single-pass sequence
 forward iterator       multi-pass forward traversal
 bidirectional iterator forward and backward traversal
 random-access iterator constant-time jumps and ordering
 contiguous iterator    random-access plus contiguous memory (C++20)
*/
entries.longDescription: Algorithms declare the minimum iterator capabilities they require. For example, std::sort needs random-access iterators, while std::find only needs input iterators.

entries.name: container iterator types
entries.description: Use mutable, const, reverse, and const-reverse iterators.
entries.longDescription: Prefer auto for local iterator declarations unless the explicit type improves teaching or API clarity.

entries.name: classic indexed loop
entries.description: Traverse an indexable sequence while retaining its index.
entries.longDescription: Use an indexed loop when the numeric position is required. Prefer range-for for simple value traversal.

entries.name: classic iterator loop
entries.description: Traverse a container explicitly through iterators.
entries.longDescription: Explicit iterators are useful when passing positions to insert/erase or when controlling traversal precisely.

entries.name: const iterator loop
entries.description: Traverse without permitting element mutation.
entries.longDescription: cbegin and cend make read-only intent explicit.

entries.name: range-based for value reference const reference
entries.description: Choose copy, mutable reference, or const reference in a range-for loop.
entries.longDescription: For non-trivial elements, const T& is the usual read-only traversal form. Use T& when mutating elements.

entries.name: structured bindings map traversal
entries.description: Traverse associative key/value pairs with structured bindings.
entries.longDescription: Use auto& or const auto& to avoid copying each pair.

entries.name: erase while iterating sequence
entries.description: Erase elements safely while traversing a sequence container.
entries.longDescription: erase returns the next valid iterator. Do not increment twice after an erase.

entries.name: erase while iterating map
entries.description: Erase associative entries safely during traversal.
entries.longDescription: Modern associative-container erase(iterator) returns the iterator following the removed element.

entries.name: reverse iterator loop
entries.description: Traverse a bidirectional or random-access sequence in reverse order.
entries.longDescription: rbegin and rend return reverse iterators and work with containers that support reverse traversal.

entries.name: std::next prev advance distance
entries.description: Move iterators generically and measure a range distance.
entries.longDescription: Complexity depends on iterator category: constant-time for random-access iterators, linear for list iterators.

entries.name: std::begin end size data generic helpers
entries.description: Use generic range helpers with arrays and containers.
entries.longDescription: std::begin and std::end enable generic traversal of built-in arrays as well as standard containers.

entries.name: back_inserter front_inserter inserter
entries.description: Adapt insertion operations into output iterators.
entries.longDescription: Insertion iterators are especially useful as destinations for copy, transform, and ranges algorithms.

entries.name: istream_iterator ostream_iterator
entries.description: Read or write sequences through stream iterators.
entries.longDescription: Stream iterators bridge formatted I/O and STL algorithms.

entries.name: ranges filter transform pipeline C++20
entries.description: Compose lazy traversal views with C++20 ranges.
entries.longDescription: Views generally do not own the underlying elements. Ensure the source range outlives the view pipeline.

entries.name: ranges subrange iterator pair
entries.description: Wrap an iterator/sentinel pair as a range.
entries.longDescription: std::ranges::subrange is useful for exposing slices without copying elements.

entries.name: Algorithm selection quick reference
entries.description: Prefer standard algorithms when they state the intent clearly.
entries.insertText:
/*
 Search:       find, find_if, count_if, any_of, all_of, none_of
 Ordering:     sort, stable_sort, partial_sort, nth_element, lower_bound
 Mutation:     remove_if + erase, std::erase_if, unique, partition
 Transform:    transform, for_each, copy, move
 Aggregation:  accumulate, reduce, minmax_element
 Sets:         set_union, set_intersection, set_difference
 C++20 ranges: std::ranges::find, sort, transform, views pipelines
*/
entries.longDescription: Algorithms work through iterators or ranges and reduce manual loop boilerplate.

entries.name: std::find and std::find_if
entries.description: Search by equality or predicate.
entries.longDescription: find_if is a general-purpose search tool for containers that do not provide a more specialized member lookup.

entries.name: count_if any_of all_of none_of
entries.description: Evaluate predicates across a range.
entries.longDescription: These algorithms express intent more directly than manual boolean accumulator loops.

entries.name: std::sort stable_sort comparator
entries.description: Sort random-access ranges with optional stability.
entries.longDescription: stable_sort preserves the relative order of equivalent elements. std::list instead uses its member sort.

entries.name: partial_sort nth_element
entries.description: Compute a sorted prefix or partition around one rank.
entries.longDescription: Use these algorithms when a fully sorted range would do unnecessary work.

entries.name: lower_bound binary_search sorted vector
entries.description: Search efficiently inside an already sorted random-access sequence.
entries.longDescription: A sorted vector can be a strong read-heavy alternative to tree containers due to compact storage and cache locality.

entries.name: erase-remove idiom pre C++20
entries.description: Remove matching sequence elements before C++20.
entries.longDescription: remove_if compacts retained elements and returns the logical new end; erase then removes the trailing range physically.

entries.name: sort unique erase deduplicate vector
entries.description: Deduplicate a vector by sorting then erasing adjacent duplicates.
entries.longDescription: Use a set instead when uniqueness must be enforced incrementally and ordering semantics are acceptable.

entries.name: partition stable_partition
entries.description: Split a range according to a predicate.
entries.longDescription: stable_partition preserves relative order within each partition but may perform more work.

entries.name: std::transform with back_inserter
entries.description: Map a range into another container.
entries.longDescription: Transform states element-wise conversion intent clearly and works with insertion iterators.

entries.name: std::for_each and std::ranges::for_each
entries.description: Apply an operation to every element.
entries.longDescription: A range-for loop can be equally readable for simple cases. Algorithms compose better in generic code.

entries.name: std::accumulate
entries.description: Fold a range sequentially into one result.
entries.longDescription: The initial value determines the accumulation type, so use 0.0 rather than 0 for floating-point sums.

entries.name: std::minmax_element
entries.description: Find minimum and maximum elements in one pass.
entries.longDescription: Always check the empty-range case before dereferencing returned iterators.

entries.name: std::copy copy_if move
entries.description: Copy filtered values or move resources into another range.
entries.longDescription: std::move algorithm moves each element; moved-from objects remain valid but their values are generally unspecified.

entries.name: set_union intersection difference
entries.description: Apply set operations to sorted ranges.
entries.longDescription: Inputs must be sorted according to the same ordering. Related algorithms include set_union, set_difference, and includes.

entries.name: std::ranges find sort projections C++20
entries.description: Use C++20 ranges algorithms and projections.
entries.longDescription: Projections can eliminate small adapter lambdas when sorting or searching by a member or accessor.

entries.name: lambda syntax quick reference
entries.description: Reference the main lambda capture forms.
entries.insertText:
/*
 []                 capture nothing
 [value]            capture one variable by value
 [&value]           capture one variable by reference
 [=]                capture used automatic variables by value
 [&]                capture used automatic variables by reference
 [&, threshold]     reference default, threshold by value
 [=, &result]       value default, result by reference
 [this]             capture this pointer
 [*this]            copy current object (C++17)
 [name = expression] init-capture (C++14)
*/
entries.longDescription: Capture deliberately. Avoid broad reference captures for callbacks that can outlive the current scope.

entries.name: captureless lambda
entries.description: Declare a lambda without external state.
entries.longDescription: Captureless lambdas are small function objects and can convert to compatible plain function pointers.

entries.name: capture by value and reference
entries.description: Mix value and reference captures explicitly.
entries.longDescription: Value captures copy state into the closure. Reference captures alias external state and require careful lifetime management.

entries.name: default captures and explicit exceptions
entries.description: Use a default capture while overriding one variable explicitly.
entries.longDescription: Prefer explicit captures in long-lived callbacks because they make dependencies and lifetimes easier to audit.

entries.name: capture this and copy object
entries.description: Distinguish capturing an object pointer from copying the object state.
entries.longDescription: [this] captures a pointer and can dangle. [*this] copies the current object into the closure when the type is copyable.

entries.name: init capture and move capture
entries.description: Initialize a closure field directly and move ownership into a callback.
entries.longDescription: Init-capture is useful for renamed variables, computed capture values, and move-only resources.

entries.name: mutable lambda state
entries.description: Permit mutation of values stored inside the closure object.
entries.longDescription: By-value captures are logically const inside operator() unless mutable is specified.

entries.name: lambda parameters return type noexcept
entries.description: Specify parameters, exception contract, and trailing return type.
entries.longDescription: A trailing return type is useful when deduction is insufficient or when documenting an interface.

entries.name: generic lambda auto parameters
entries.description: Declare a templated call operator through auto parameters.
entries.longDescription: Generic lambdas are concise reusable function objects for algorithms and local helpers.

entries.name: templated lambda C++20
entries.description: Declare explicit template parameters on a lambda.
entries.longDescription: C++20 templated lambdas are useful when auto parameters alone cannot express the intended constraints or explicit template arguments.

entries.name: constexpr lambda
entries.description: Use a lambda during constant evaluation when its body permits it.
entries.longDescription: Lambdas can participate in compile-time computation and local metaprogramming helpers.

entries.name: recursive lambda self parameter
entries.description: Implement a local recursive lambda without std::function.
entries.longDescription: Passing the closure to itself avoids type-erasure overhead and keeps the helper local.

entries.name: lambda immediately invoked
entries.description: Use an immediately invoked lambda to compute a const value with structured control flow.
entries.longDescription: This pattern keeps temporary setup logic local while allowing const initialization.

entries.name: captureless lambda to function pointer
entries.description: Convert a captureless lambda to a compatible function pointer.
entries.longDescription: A lambda with captures cannot convert to a plain function pointer because it needs closure state.

entries.name: std::function callback storage
entries.description: Store heterogeneous copyable callbacks behind one signature.
entries.longDescription: std::function performs type erasure and may allocate. Use it when runtime callback replacement is useful and the overhead is acceptable.

entries.name: template callback parameter zero overhead
entries.description: Accept an arbitrary callback without std::function type erasure.
entries.longDescription: A forwarding template is suitable for hot paths and compile-time composition when ABI stability is not required.

entries.name: std::invoke function member pointer callable
entries.description: Invoke functions, function objects, member functions, or data-member pointers uniformly.
entries.longDescription: std::invoke is a useful generic dispatch primitive for callback frameworks and adapter utilities.

entries.name: std::bind and lambda preferred
entries.description: Bind arguments to a callable and compare with the clearer lambda form.
entries.longDescription: std::bind remains available, but lambdas usually make captures, argument order, and lifetimes easier to read.

entries.name: callback list event dispatch
entries.description: Store and emit a simple list of callbacks.
entries.longDescription: For production event systems, add disconnection tokens, exception policy, reentrancy rules, and thread-safety decisions.

entries.name: avoid dangling reference capture
entries.description: Recognize the lifetime hazard of returning a reference-capturing callback.
entries.longDescription: Reference captures are safe only while the referenced objects remain alive. This is especially important for deferred, GUI, and threaded callbacks.

entries.name: weak_ptr callback guard
entries.description: Avoid extending lifetime or dereferencing a destroyed shared object from a callback.
entries.longDescription: weak_ptr is a common technique for callbacks registered into systems that may outlive the observed object.

entries.name: thread lambda value capture
entries.description: Move owned state into a worker thread callback.
entries.longDescription: Avoid capturing stack references unless the thread is joined before those references can expire and concurrent access is synchronized.

entries.name: jthread stop token callback C++20
entries.description: Use a cooperative cancellation token inside a C++20 jthread callback.
entries.longDescription: std::jthread requests stop and joins automatically at destruction, which is safer than unmanaged thread shutdown paths.

entries.name: move-only callback note C++23
entries.description: Document the C++23 move-only callback wrapper.
entries.insertText:
/*
 C++23: std::move_only_function<void()> can store move-only callables.
 Use it when a callback owns move-only state and copying is not required.
 Availability depends on the selected standard library implementation.
*/
entries.longDescription: std::function requires copyable targets. std::move_only_function addresses callbacks that intentionally own move-only resources.

entries.name: read entire text file
entries.description: Read a complete text file into one std::string.
entries.longDescription: Use this when the file is small enough to hold in memory, for example configuration files, templates, JSON payloads, or text resources.

entries.name: std::filesystem path and recursive iteration
entries.description: Manipulate paths and enumerate files with the standard filesystem library.
entries.longDescription: std::filesystem is the standard C++17 API for paths, directory traversal, metadata queries, copy, rename, and removal operations.

entries.name: std::filesystem copy rename remove
entries.description: Copy, rename, and remove files with std::filesystem.
entries.longDescription: Prefer std::filesystem over ad hoc platform commands when working with regular files and directories.

entries.name: atomic-ish config replace
entries.description: Write a temporary configuration file and replace the previous file only after the write succeeds.
entries.longDescription: Writing to a temporary file before replacement reduces the risk of leaving a partially-written configuration file. Exact replacement semantics differ between operating systems, so production code may need a platform-specific final replace step.

entries.name: stream state validation
entries.description: Check stream status after parsing or writing.
entries.longDescription: Stream extraction operations communicate malformed or missing data through the stream state. Check the state instead of assuming parsing succeeded.

entries.name: nlohmann json dependency note
entries.description: Document the common JSON for Modern C++ dependency.
entries.longDescription: nlohmann/json is a third-party C++ library. It is not part of the C++ standard library. It provides a convenient JSON value type, parsing helpers, serialization helpers, and conversions.

entries.name: parse JSON file with nlohmann json
entries.description: Parse a JSON configuration file through std::ifstream.
entries.longDescription: The JSON parser can consume an input stream directly. Catch nlohmann::json::parse_error when malformed user configuration must be reported cleanly.

entries.name: safe JSON field access
entries.description: Read required and optional JSON fields deliberately.
entries.longDescription: Use at() for required fields, value() for optional fields with defaults, and contains() when the presence of a member changes behavior.

entries.name: write JSON file pretty print
entries.description: Serialize a JSON object to disk with indentation.
entries.longDescription: dump(4) produces human-readable indentation. Use compact dump() without an indentation argument for smaller payloads sent over a network.

entries.name: JSON parse error handling
entries.description: Report malformed JSON without crashing the application.
entries.longDescription: The parse_error exception includes diagnostic text and a byte position. This is useful for configuration editors and operator-facing tools.

entries.name: JSON parse without exceptions
entries.description: Parse JSON while returning a discarded value on failure.
entries.longDescription: Disable exceptions only when a simple success/failure result is sufficient. In this mode, detailed parse diagnostics are not available.

entries.name: custom type to_json from_json
entries.description: Serialize and deserialize a domain structure with nlohmann/json.
entries.longDescription: Free to_json and from_json functions make domain structures easier to exchange with JavaScript frontends and configuration files.

entries.name: minimal key value config parser
entries.description: Parse a simple key=value file without an external dependency.
entries.longDescription: A small parser is sufficient for controlled internal files. For comments, escaping, sections, Unicode, validation, or round-trip editing, use a dedicated configuration library.

entries.name: Boost PropertyTree read INI
entries.description: Read an INI file with Boost.PropertyTree.
entries.longDescription: Boost.PropertyTree provides read_ini and write_ini helpers. It is useful when a project already depends on Boost and a lightweight hierarchical configuration tree is sufficient.

entries.name: toml++ parse file
entries.description: Parse a typed TOML configuration file with toml++.
entries.longDescription: toml++ is a third-party parser for TOML configuration files. TOML is useful when humans frequently edit settings and typed values matter.

entries.name: environment variable override
entries.description: Override a configuration field from an environment variable.
entries.longDescription: Environment variables are useful for deployment overrides, CI jobs, and secrets that should not be committed to a configuration file.

entries.name: simple CSV line parser
entries.description: Split a simple comma-separated line.
entries.longDescription: This minimal parser does not handle quoted commas, escaped quotes, or multiline fields. Use a dedicated CSV library for general CSV input.

entries.name: write delimited measurements
entries.description: Write a compact CSV-like measurement log.
entries.longDescription: Delimited text remains practical for test benches, spreadsheets, and quick data analysis. Define quoting and decimal conventions explicitly if fields can contain text.

entries.name: binary vector write
entries.description: Write raw byte storage to a binary file.
entries.longDescription: Raw binary files are useful for captures and firmware images. Define endianness, versioning, and record boundaries when the format must remain stable.

entries.name: binary POD warning
entries.description: Document why dumping arbitrary C++ objects is unsafe.
entries.insertText:
/*
 Avoid writing an arbitrary C++ object with:
 output.write(reinterpret_cast<const char *>(&object), sizeof(object));

 Padding, endianness, pointer members, virtual tables, ABI changes,
 compiler differences, and version changes can make the file unstable.
 Serialize fields explicitly or use a serialization format/library.
*/
entries.longDescription: Direct memory dumps are only appropriate for tightly-controlled trivial layouts with an explicit binary contract.

entries.name: serial and USB API selection quick reference
entries.description: Choose an API according to the device and portability requirement.
entries.insertText:
/*
 Serial / UART over COM or tty:
   - portable C++ wrapper: Boost.Asio serial_port
   - Windows native API: CreateFile + DCB + ReadFile/WriteFile
   - POSIX native API: open + termios + read/write

 USB device access:
   - generic USB transfers: libusb
   - USB HID or Bluetooth HID: HIDAPI
   - vendor SDK / OS driver API when required by the device
*/
entries.longDescription: C++ does not provide a standard serial-port or USB API. Use a cross-platform library or the operating-system API appropriate for the target.

entries.name: Boost.Asio open and configure serial port
entries.description: Open a serial port portably with Boost.Asio.
entries.longDescription: Boost.Asio exposes a portable serial_port abstraction. A Windows name such as COM3 and a POSIX name such as /dev/ttyUSB0 identify the device.

entries.name: Boost.Asio serial write
entries.description: Write a complete serial buffer.
entries.longDescription: Use boost::asio::write when the complete buffer must be sent before continuing. For GUI or concurrent applications, prefer asynchronous operations.

entries.name: Boost.Asio serial read line
entries.description: Read a line-terminated serial frame.
entries.longDescription: read_until is convenient for text protocols. For binary frames, maintain a byte buffer and implement explicit frame extraction.

entries.name: Boost.Asio async serial read_some
entries.description: Start an asynchronous serial read.
entries.longDescription: Asynchronous reads avoid blocking the calling thread. Keep buffers alive until the completion handler runs.

entries.name: Win32 open configure COM port
entries.description: Open and configure a Windows COM port with the Win32 API.
entries.longDescription: CreateFile opens Windows communications resources. The \.\COM12 form also works for COM port numbers greater than 9.

entries.name: Win32 COM timeouts and read write
entries.description: Configure serial timeouts and exchange bytes on Windows.
entries.longDescription: For responsive applications, consider overlapped I/O instead of synchronous ReadFile and WriteFile calls.

entries.name: POSIX open configure tty serial port
entries.description: Open and configure a serial tty on Linux or another POSIX platform.
entries.longDescription: termios is the POSIX native serial configuration API. Add error handling and select, poll, or asynchronous integration according to the application architecture.

entries.name: libusb initialize open VID PID
entries.description: Initialize libusb and open a USB device by vendor and product ID.
entries.longDescription: libusb provides user-space access to USB devices. A production implementation should inspect descriptors, handle kernel-driver ownership where relevant, release interfaces, close the handle, and exit the context.

entries.name: libusb bulk transfer
entries.description: Exchange data through a USB bulk endpoint.
entries.longDescription: The endpoint address determines the direction. Bulk transfers are common for devices exchanging larger reliable byte streams.

entries.name: libusb control transfer
entries.description: Send a USB control transfer.
entries.longDescription: Control transfers are commonly used for setup, vendor commands, and small structured exchanges over endpoint zero.

entries.name: libusb cleanup
entries.description: Release a libusb interface and close the library cleanly.
entries.longDescription: Pair resource acquisition with cleanup paths. RAII wrappers are appropriate when libusb is used throughout a larger C++ application.

entries.name: libusb async transfer note
entries.description: Document when to use asynchronous USB transfers.
entries.insertText:
/*
 libusb also exposes an asynchronous transfer API:
   libusb_alloc_transfer
   libusb_fill_bulk_transfer / libusb_fill_interrupt_transfer
   libusb_submit_transfer
   libusb_handle_events
   libusb_cancel_transfer
   libusb_free_transfer

 Use it when synchronous transfers would block an event loop or when
 several transfers must remain in flight concurrently.
*/
entries.longDescription: The asynchronous libusb API is more powerful but also more complex than the synchronous transfer helpers.

entries.name: HIDAPI open read write
entries.description: Communicate with a USB HID or Bluetooth HID device portably.
entries.longDescription: HIDAPI is appropriate for HID-class USB and Bluetooth devices when direct HID reports are sufficient.

entries.name: C++ backend frontend architecture
entries.description: Outline a practical local or embedded web architecture.
entries.insertText:
/*
 Browser frontend (HTML / CSS / JavaScript)
        |
        | fetch() HTTP requests + JSON payloads
        v
 C++ backend REST API
        |
        +-- domain logic
        +-- serial / USB / TCP devices
        +-- configuration files

 Typical endpoints:
   GET  /api/status
   POST /api/config
   POST /api/command
*/
entries.longDescription: A browser cannot call C++ functions directly. Expose an HTTP, WebSocket, or similar network boundary and exchange explicit payloads such as JSON.

entries.name: Boost.Asio TCP client
entries.description: Connect to a TCP server and exchange bytes.
entries.longDescription: TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream. Define framing explicitly, for example lines, length prefixes, or a higher-level protocol such as HTTP.

entries.name: Boost.Asio TCP server accept
entries.description: Listen for one incoming TCP connection.
entries.longDescription: A production server typically uses asynchronous accept and per-connection state objects rather than blocking on one client.

entries.name: Boost.Asio UDP send receive
entries.description: Send a datagram and receive a response.
entries.longDescription: UDP exchanges independent datagrams without TCP ordering or delivery guarantees. It suits telemetry, discovery, and controlled low-latency protocols.

entries.name: libcurl HTTP GET capture string
entries.description: Perform an HTTP GET request and collect the response body.
entries.longDescription: libcurl is a mature transfer library. The easy interface is synchronous; use the multi interface when several transfers or event-loop integration are required.

entries.name: libcurl POST JSON
entries.description: Send a JSON request body with libcurl.
entries.longDescription: For HTTPS, configure certificate verification correctly. Do not disable peer or host verification in production code.

entries.name: libcurl easy versus multi reference
entries.description: Choose between synchronous and asynchronous-style libcurl interfaces.
entries.insertText:
/*
 libcurl easy interface:
   curl_easy_init
   curl_easy_setopt
   curl_easy_perform      // blocking transfer
   curl_easy_cleanup

 libcurl multi interface:
   curl_multi_init
   curl_multi_add_handle
   curl_multi_perform
   curl_multi_poll
   curl_multi_remove_handle
   curl_multi_cleanup
*/
entries.longDescription: The easy interface is appropriate for simple blocking requests. The multi interface allows several transfers and application-driven polling in a single thread.

entries.name: cpp-httplib REST GET endpoint
entries.description: Expose a JSON status endpoint from a small C++ HTTP server.
entries.longDescription: cpp-httplib is a compact third-party header-only HTTP library. It is convenient for local tools, prototypes, and moderate HTTP services.

entries.name: cpp-httplib REST POST JSON endpoint
entries.description: Parse a JSON command received from a JavaScript frontend.
entries.longDescription: Validate payloads and return explicit HTTP status codes. Do not trust data received from a browser or another network client.

entries.name: cpp-httplib static frontend and CORS
entries.description: Serve static frontend files and add a CORS header when needed.
entries.longDescription: For development, the frontend and backend may use different local ports and require CORS headers. For production, serve a built frontend from the same origin when practical.

entries.name: cpp-httplib server thread and stop
entries.description: Run a small HTTP server on a dedicated thread and stop it cleanly.
entries.longDescription: Keep shutdown explicit. Integrate error reporting and ownership rules if the server shares application state with GUI or device threads.

entries.name: browser fetch GET status
entries.description: Fetch a C++ backend status endpoint from JavaScript.
entries.longDescription: This JavaScript counterpart shows the browser side of a C++ REST backend. The frontend consumes JSON rather than linking directly to C++ code.

entries.name: browser fetch POST command
entries.description: Send a JSON command from JavaScript to a C++ backend.
entries.longDescription: Use explicit REST endpoints for user actions, settings updates, and device commands.

entries.name: Boost.Beast WebSocket server session skeleton
entries.description: Accept and echo one WebSocket message with Boost.Beast.
entries.longDescription: WebSockets are suitable for live telemetry, notifications, and bidirectional updates. Boost.Beast builds HTTP and WebSocket primitives on Boost.Asio.

entries.name: communication technology selection quick reference
entries.description: Choose the transport and protocol layer deliberately.
entries.insertText:
/*
 UART / serial       simple point-to-point byte stream; define framing
 USB CDC serial      appears as COM or tty; use the serial API
 USB HID             HIDAPI for HID reports
 Generic USB         libusb or a vendor SDK
 Ethernet / Wi-Fi    TCP, UDP, HTTP, WebSocket after network connection exists
 Bluetooth Classic   RFCOMM / sockets or platform SDK
 Bluetooth Low Energy GATT APIs through platform SDK or a BLE library
*/
entries.longDescription: Separate the physical transport from the application protocol. For example, Wi-Fi can carry the same HTTP or TCP protocol as wired Ethernet.

entries.name: C++ standard connectivity scope note
entries.description: Document which communication layers are outside the C++ standard library.
entries.insertText:
/*
 The C++ standard library does not configure Wi-Fi adapters, pair Bluetooth
 devices, open serial ports, or perform raw USB transfers.

 Use:
   - portable libraries such as Boost.Asio, libcurl, libusb, HIDAPI
   - operating-system APIs such as Win32 COM, Native Wifi, Winsock Bluetooth,
     POSIX termios, or BlueZ
   - vendor SDKs when a device requires a custom driver or protocol
*/
entries.longDescription: Keeping platform-specific code behind narrow interfaces makes the rest of the application easier to test and port.

entries.name: newline delimited UART protocol
entries.description: Build and parse a simple line-oriented serial protocol.
entries.longDescription: Line protocols are easy to debug manually. For arbitrary binary payloads or high throughput, use explicit binary framing.

entries.name: length prefixed binary frame
entries.description: Define a compact framed binary message.
entries.longDescription: Define byte order, size limits, CRC coverage, and resynchronization behavior explicitly. Do not transmit compiler-dependent object layouts without a wire-format contract.

entries.name: CRC16 Modbus helper
entries.description: Calculate a CRC-16 suitable for many serial protocols.
entries.longDescription: Use the CRC polynomial and initialization required by the actual protocol. CRC detects accidental corruption; it is not a security mechanism.

entries.name: byte stream accumulator parser
entries.description: Accumulate partial reads before extracting complete frames.
entries.longDescription: Serial ports and TCP sockets are byte streams: one read does not necessarily correspond to one message. Accumulate bytes and parse complete frames explicitly.

entries.name: Wi-Fi uses regular IP sockets after connection
entries.description: Use TCP, UDP, HTTP, or WebSocket normally once the operating system is connected to Wi-Fi.
entries.insertText:
/*
 Once the operating system has joined a Wi-Fi network, application traffic
 normally uses the same IP APIs as Ethernet:
   - Boost.Asio TCP / UDP sockets
   - libcurl HTTP client
   - cpp-httplib or Boost.Beast server
   - WebSocket for live bidirectional updates
*/
entries.longDescription: Wi-Fi association and IP application traffic are different layers. Many applications only need the regular socket layer.

entries.name: Windows Native Wifi enumerate interfaces
entries.description: Enumerate enabled Wi-Fi adapters through the Windows Native Wifi API.
entries.longDescription: Native Wifi is the Windows API for enumerating interfaces, scanning, inspecting profiles, and managing WLAN state. Free buffers returned by WLAN functions with WlanFreeMemory.

entries.name: Windows Native Wifi scan available networks note
entries.description: Document the asynchronous WLAN scan flow on Windows.
entries.insertText:
/*
 Windows Native Wifi scan flow:
   1. WlanOpenHandle
   2. WlanEnumInterfaces
   3. WlanRegisterNotification for WLAN_NOTIFICATION_SOURCE_ACM
   4. WlanScan(interfaceGuid, ...)
   5. wait for wlan_notification_acm_scan_complete or timeout
   6. WlanGetAvailableNetworkList
   7. WlanFreeMemory for returned lists
*/
entries.longDescription: WlanScan returns immediately. Treat scanning as an asynchronous system operation rather than assuming the result list is updated before the call returns.

entries.name: Bluetooth API selection quick reference
entries.description: Choose a Bluetooth path according to the profile and platform.
entries.insertText:
/*
 Bluetooth HID device:
   - HIDAPI may be sufficient

 Bluetooth Classic RFCOMM / custom sockets:
   - Windows: Winsock Bluetooth (AF_BTH)
   - Linux: BlueZ socket APIs or a higher-level library

 Bluetooth Low Energy:
   - use GATT APIs through the platform SDK or a BLE library
   - model services, characteristics, notifications, and pairing explicitly
*/
entries.longDescription: Bluetooth is not one generic byte stream API. The appropriate interface depends on the profile: HID, RFCOMM, or BLE GATT.

entries.name: Windows Winsock Bluetooth RFCOMM socket skeleton
entries.description: Open a Bluetooth RFCOMM socket on Windows.
entries.longDescription: This is a Windows-specific Bluetooth Classic RFCOMM outline. Add discovery, pairing, error handling, and lifetime management for a production implementation.

entries.name: Linux BlueZ RFCOMM socket skeleton
entries.description: Open a Bluetooth RFCOMM socket through Linux BlueZ headers.
entries.longDescription: This is a Linux-specific Bluetooth Classic RFCOMM outline. BLE uses a different GATT-oriented model.

entries.name: BLE GATT conceptual flow
entries.description: Document the BLE service and characteristic workflow.
entries.insertText:
/*
 BLE GATT client flow:
   1. discover or select peripheral
   2. pair / bond if required
   3. connect
   4. discover services
   5. discover characteristics
   6. read / write characteristic values
   7. subscribe to notifications or indications
   8. disconnect cleanly

 Implement with the target platform SDK or a BLE library.
*/
entries.longDescription: BLE communication is structured around GATT services and characteristics rather than a generic serial byte stream.

entries.name: __declspec(dllexport)
entries.description: Export a symbol from a Windows DLL.
entries.insertText: __declspec(dllexport)
entries.longDescription: Put this on exported classes, functions, or variables in the DLL build.

entries.name: __declspec(dllimport)
entries.description: Import a symbol from a Windows DLL.
entries.insertText: __declspec(dllimport)
entries.longDescription: Put this in client code or common headers consumed by applications using the DLL.

entries.name: extern "C"
entries.description: Expose a stable C ABI from C++ code.
entries.insertText: extern "C"
entries.longDescription: This avoids C++ name mangling and is extremely useful for plugin boundaries and runtime loading.

entries.name: DLL export macro
entries.description: Windows export/import macro pattern for C++.
entries.insertText:
#ifdef BUILDING_MY_DLL
#define MY_API __declspec(dllexport)
#else
#define MY_API __declspec(dllimport)
#endif
entries.longDescription: Reusable pattern for headers shared by the DLL project and all client projects.

entries.name: Exported class
entries.description: Typical exported C++ class.
entries.longDescription: Good for tightly coupled C++ consumers, though a pure C API is often more stable across compilers.

entries.name: Extern C API bridge
entries.description: C API bridge exported from C++.
entries.longDescription: A stable boundary for plugins, scripting, and applications compiled with other languages or toolchains.

entries.name: Factory / destroy pair
entries.description: Export factory functions for an interface-based API.
entries.longDescription: Common plugin pattern when the host loads the DLL at runtime and interacts through a narrow interface.

entries.name: Exported callback registration
entries.description: Let the host register a C callback into the DLL.
entries.longDescription: Useful when the DLL must push diagnostics, events, or status messages back to the application.

entries.name: LoadLibrary + exported factory
entries.description: Runtime-load a C++ plugin through a C factory API on Windows.
entries.longDescription: Recommended when you want C++ internals but a predictable runtime loading boundary.

entries.name: dlopen / dlsym shared object
entries.description: Load a shared object at runtime on Linux.
entries.longDescription: Linux equivalent for runtime-loaded shared libraries. Keep exported entry points C-compatible when possible.

entries.name: #define object-like macro
entries.description: Define a simple symbolic replacement.
entries.insertText: #define MAX_SAMPLES 256
entries.longDescription: Object-like macros perform token substitution before compilation. They are useful for compile-time constants and conditional-compilation flags, but prefer typed constants in C++ when a macro is not required.

entries.name: #define function-like macro
entries.description: Wrap an expression-like macro with defensive parentheses.
entries.insertText: #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
entries.longDescription: Function-like macros should parenthesize both parameters and the full expansion to reduce precedence bugs. They still evaluate arguments multiple times, so they are not a drop-in replacement for real functions.

entries.name: multi-statement macro do { } while (0)
entries.description: Package several statements into one macro safely.
entries.insertText: #define SAFE_FREE(ptr)                do                                 {                                      free(ptr);                         (ptr) = NULL;                  } while (0)
entries.longDescription: The do { } while (0) pattern makes a multi-statement macro behave like a single statement in if/else contexts. This is one of the most important defensive macro idioms in C and C++.

entries.name: __VA_ARGS__ logging macro
entries.description: Forward a variable number of macro arguments.
entries.insertText:
#define LOG_ERROR(fmt, ...)     fprintf(stderr, "[ERROR] " fmt "
", __VA_ARGS__)
entries.longDescription: __VA_ARGS__ expands to the comma-separated tail arguments supplied to a variadic macro. This is the classic C99 and C++11 mechanism for macro-based logging, tracing, and lightweight wrappers.

entries.name: __VA_OPT__ optional comma
entries.description: Keep a variadic macro valid even when no extra argument is supplied.
entries.insertText:
#define LOG_INFO(fmt, ...)     fprintf(stderr, "[INFO] " fmt "
" __VA_OPT__(,) __VA_ARGS__)
entries.longDescription: __VA_OPT__ is the standard way in modern preprocessors to inject a token such as a comma only when the variadic part is non-empty. It is standard in C++20 and C23, but availability depends on the language mode and compiler.

entries.name: # stringizing operator
entries.description: Turn the raw macro argument tokens into a string literal.
entries.insertText:
#define TO_TEXT(x) #x

const char *name = TO_TEXT(DeviceReady);
entries.longDescription: The # operator stringizes the exact argument tokens after macro-parameter substitution rules are applied. This is useful for diagnostics, generated names, and table-driven code.

entries.name: ## token pasting operator
entries.description: Concatenate tokens during macro expansion.
entries.insertText:
#define REGISTER_HANDLER(name) Handle_##name

void REGISTER_HANDLER(Start)(void);
entries.longDescription: ## pastes adjacent tokens into one new token. It is useful for generated identifiers, register maps, and X-macro code generation, but it can reduce readability if overused.

entries.name: #if / #elif / defined
entries.description: Compile code only when a symbol or feature flag is enabled.
entries.insertText:
#if defined(_WIN32)
    #define PLATFORM_NAME "Windows"
#elif defined(__linux__)
    #define PLATFORM_NAME "Linux"
#else
    #define PLATFORM_NAME "Unknown"
#endif
entries.longDescription: Conditional compilation is the core preprocessor mechanism for platform selection, feature flags, and compiler workarounds. defined(NAME) is clearer and safer than relying on a macro value that may not exist.

entries.name: #ifdef __cplusplus bridge
entries.description: Expose C linkage when a header is included from C++.
entries.longDescription: This is the standard shared-header bridge for C libraries consumed by both C and C++. The __cplusplus macro is predefined only in C++ translation units.

entries.name: header guard
entries.description: Prevent multiple inclusion with #ifndef / #define / #endif.
entries.insertText:
#ifndef DEVICE_DRIVER_H
#define DEVICE_DRIVER_H

/* declarations */

#endif /* DEVICE_DRIVER_H */
entries.longDescription: Header guards are the portable baseline for repeated inclusion safety. They work in both C and C++ and remain relevant even when some compilers also support #pragma once.

entries.name: #pragma once
entries.description: Ask the compiler to include a header only once per translation unit.
entries.insertText: #pragma once
entries.longDescription: #pragma once is widely supported and concise, but it is still a compiler directive rather than a core-language mechanism. Some teams keep classic header guards for maximum portability or style consistency.

entries.name: #pragma pack(push, 1)
entries.description: Temporarily change structure packing.
entries.longDescription: Packing pragmas are common in binary protocols and hardware-facing layouts, but they should be used carefully. They can change ABI, alignment, and performance characteristics.

entries.name: #pragma message
entries.description: Emit a build-time informational message.
entries.insertText: #pragma message("Building with diagnostic instrumentation enabled")
entries.longDescription: A compiler message pragma can help surface configuration details during a build. Support and exact formatting vary by compiler.

entries.name: _Pragma inside a macro
entries.description: Inject a pragma from within another macro.
entries.insertText:
#define DO_PRAGMA(x) _Pragma(#x)
#define TODO_MESSAGE(text) DO_PRAGMA(message(text))

TODO_MESSAGE("verify register map before release")
entries.longDescription: _Pragma is the macro-friendly form of pragma in standard C and C++. It is especially useful when you need to generate pragmas from another macro layer.

entries.name: #error hard stop
entries.description: Abort compilation when a required condition is not satisfied.
entries.insertText:
#ifndef PROJECT_VERSION
#error PROJECT_VERSION must be defined before including this header
#endif
entries.longDescription: #error is a deliberate compile-time stop. It is appropriate when a configuration is invalid or when a contract must be enforced before code generation continues.

entries.name: X-macro table
entries.description: Define one master list and expand it in several ways.
entries.longDescription: X macros keep one authoritative item list and reuse it to generate enums, strings, lookup tables, declarations, or command descriptors. They are extremely powerful in embedded and systems code when duplication must stay tightly controlled.

entries.name: __FILE__ / __LINE__ / __DATE__ / __TIME__
entries.description: Reference build and source-location metadata supplied by the preprocessor.
entries.insertText:
fprintf(stderr, "Fault at %s:%d (built %s %s)
", __FILE__, __LINE__, __DATE__, __TIME__);
entries.longDescription: These predefined macros are useful for diagnostics and lightweight trace output. Be aware that __DATE__ and __TIME__ can harm reproducible builds because they embed the build timestamp.

entries.name: CVICALLBACK
entries.description: CVI callback specifier.
entries.insertText: CVICALLBACK
entries.longDescription: Used by LabWindows/CVI for callback signatures such as panel, timer, and control callbacks.

entries.name: CVIFUNC
entries.description: CVI exported function specifier.
entries.insertText: CVIFUNC
entries.longDescription: Commonly used in CVI headers to mark externally visible functions.

entries.name: CVI callback skeleton

entries.name: LoadPanel pattern

entries.description: Read and write CVI control values.

entries.name: QObject
entries.description: Base class for most Qt object hierarchies.
entries.insertText: QObject
entries.longDescription: QObject provides parent-child ownership, the meta-object system, signals and slots, and event delivery.

entries.name: Q_OBJECT
entries.description: Enable Qt meta-object features in a QObject-derived class.
entries.insertText: Q_OBJECT
entries.longDescription: Required for custom signals, slots, properties, and runtime type information generated by moc.

entries.name: signals
entries.description: Qt signal section in a class declaration.
entries.insertText:
signals:

entries.longDescription: Signals declare notifications emitted by a QObject-based class.

entries.name: slots
entries.description: Qt slot section in a class declaration.

public slots:
